entry.title: Smarter Slotting in SAP EWM: What If Products That Travel Together Could Live Together?
entry.content:
Smarter Slotting in SAP EWM: What If Products That Travel Together Could Live Together?

An idea for extending ML-based slotting with product affinity

Introduction

Warehouse slotting has always been about putting the right product in the right place. But as warehouses become more intelligent, perhaps the question should no longer stop there.

What if two products are both stored in the right area, but they are frequently picked together and located far apart?

From an individual product perspective, the slotting decision may be completely correct. From an order-picking perspective, however, there may still be room for improvement.

In my work around SAP EWM, I have often seen how a warehouse decision can look perfectly logical when we look at one product at a time. But warehouse operations rarely executed one product at a time. Pickers move through orders, and orders create relationships between products.

That made me think about whether we are sometimes optimizing the location of individual products without fully optimizing the journey created by the order.

This led me to an idea: could product affinity become another signal that complements SAP EWM’s existing Machine Learning–based slotting?

Not as a replacement for the existing slotting logic, but as another layer of intelligence on top of it.

I call this idea Smarter Neighbors.

SAP EWM can already use machine learning to answer an important warehouse question:

Where should this product live?

But there is another question warehouses deal with every day:

What products usually go together?

What SAP EWM Already Does

SAP EWM’s Slotting by Machine Learning is already a useful capability. Through SAP’s Intelligent Scenario Lifecycle Management (ISLM) framework, it can analyze warehouse and product data and propose storage parameters such as the Storage Type Indicator, Storage Section Indicator, and Putaway Control Indicator.

The idea is straightforward: instead of manually deciding how a product should be classified based on expected movement and characteristics, the model learns from existing warehouse data and recommends an appropriate storage concept.

That is a meaningful step forward.

But the question I started exploring is whether the product itself is only one part of the story.

Because a warehouse does not ultimately pick products in isolation.

It picks orders.

What If We Looked at the Relationship Between Products?

Consider two products, Product A and Product B.

Both are fast movers, so the ML model can correctly identify them and place them in the appropriate fast-pick area.

Now imagine that 70% of the orders containing Product A also contain Product B.

If A is located at one end of the fast-pick area and B is at the other, the picker still must walk between them.

Both products were individually slotted correctly.

But the relationship between them was not considered.

This is where product affinity becomes interesting.

Instead of asking only:

“How fast does this product move?”

We could also ask:

“Which other products does this product usually move with?”

Product affinity, or correlated slotting, uses historical order patterns to identify products that frequently occur together. Those relationships could then potentially be used to position products closer to each other.

The objective isn’t simply to find products that are popular. It is to understand which products repeatedly participate in the same warehouse journeys.

A Different Layer of Intelligence: “Smarter Neighbors”

I think of this idea as Smarter Neighbors.

The existing ML-based slotting model could continue deciding the type of location a product should have — for example, fast-pick, bulk, or slower-moving storage.

An additional affinity layer could then look at order history and help optimize the physical proximity of products within that broader zone.

In simple terms:

ML slotting could decide the neighborhood, while affinity could help decide the neighbors.

That distinction is important to me.

I would not want affinity to override the fundamental storage strategy. A product should not suddenly move to a completely different storage area simply because it is frequently ordered with another product.

Instead, affinity could act as an additional signal for optimizing placement within an appropriate storage concept.

This creates a two-level decision:

Storage strategy → Where should the product live?

Product affinity → Who should it live closer to?

How Could It Work?

The first step would be to analyze confirmed outbound order history and identify which products frequently appear on the same orders.

From this data, we could calculate an affinity score between products and identify strong relationships.

For example, if Product A and Product B repeatedly appear together across a significant number of orders, the system could recognize that relationship and consider it when determining their final placement.

The existing slotting logic would still determine the broader storage concept.

Affinity would then become another input when deciding where the product should ideally sit within that zone.

There is also an important rule for situations where the two signals disagree.

Suppose Product A is a very fast mover, while its strongest affinity partner, Product B, is a slow-moving product.

It probably would not make sense to move Product B into the fast-pick area simply because the two products are frequently ordered together.

So, my initial thinking would be simple:

Velocity and product characteristics determine the storage zone; product affinity helps optimize proximity within that zone.

This separation could also make the approach easier to govern. The warehouse can retain the existing storage logic while using affinity as a controlled optimization layer.

Why I Think of the Separation Matters

From a practical EWM perspective, I would be cautious about making this an automated relocation mechanism from day one.

A mathematically strong affinity relationship does not automatically mean that two products should be physically adjacent.

There may be other considerations:

  • Storage capacity
  • Replenishment frequency
  • Product dimensions and weight
  • Handling requirements
  • Hazardous-material restrictions
  • Equipment requirements
  • Temperature or storage conditions
  • Operational constraints
  • Warehouse supervisor experience

A model may identify a strong relationship between two products, but the warehouse still needs to decide whether that relationship is operationally meaningful.

That is why I see Smarter Neighbors as a recommendation layer first, rather than an autonomous relocation mechanism.

The system could identify the relationship, propose a placement adjustment, and allow warehouse operations to validate the recommendation before execution.

The Interesting Part: SAP Already Has Some of the Building Blocks

This is also why I think the idea is worth exploring from an SAP perspective.

SAP’s existing ML capabilities around EWM use the ISLM framework, while HANA’s Predictive Analysis Library (PAL) provides analytical capabilities that include association-rule mining such as Apriori-based algorithms.

Association-rule mining is designed to identify relationships and co-occurrence patterns in datasets.

And that is essentially what we are trying to understand here:

Which products tend to appear together?

So, this isn’t necessarily about inventing completely new technology.

It could be about applying existing analytical capability to another warehouse problem.

The interesting question is how such a capability could relate to the existing EWM slotting process in a way that remains practical, explainable, and operationally controlled.

Could This Become Another ML Signal for Slotting?

This is where I see an interesting product opportunity.

Today, intelligent slotting can largely be thought of at a product level:

  • How fast does the item move?
  • What are its physical characteristics?
  • What storage concept does it require?
  • What storage parameters should be assigned?

What if future intelligent slotting could consider another dimension:

How do products behave together in actual customer orders?

The recommendation could potentially move beyond simply saying:

Put Product A in Zone X.

It could say something more like:

Put Product A in Zone X, preferably closer to Products B and C because they frequently travel together.

That would introduce a different dimension of intelligence into slotting.

The system would not only understand the characteristics and movement of an individual product.

It would begin to understand the relationship between products within the order flow.

Where Would I Start with a Pilot?

I wouldn’t try this across an entire warehouse initially.

I’d start with an area where multi-line orders are common.

Potential candidates could include:

  • E-commerce
  • Kitting operations
  • Recurring B2B replenishment
  • Spare parts
  • Promotional product combinations

The pilot could compare the existing placement with an affinity-adjusted placement while keeping the underlying product classification unchanged.

The primary measurement could be simple:

Pick-path distance per order.

Other useful measurements could include picker travel time, lines picked per hour, order cycle time, and potentially congestion within the picking area.

But I will start with one simple question:

Did the affinity-adjusted placement reduce the distance the picker had to travel?

If product classification remains unchanged but average travel distance decreases, that would provide an early indication that the additional affinity layer is contributing real value.

I would also want the pilot to run under controlled conditions. Product relocation should not happen simply because an algorithm identifies a correlation. The recommendation should be reviewed against warehouse constraints and operational experience.

Why Affinity Could Need a Different Learning Cycle

There is another aspect of this idea that I find particularly interesting.

Product velocity may change gradually, while product relationships can change much faster.

A promotion can suddenly cause two products to appear together frequently.

A new bundle can create a new relationship.

Seasonality can change order patterns.

Customer behavior can shift.

A product that historically had little relationship with another product may suddenly become a frequent companion.

This suggests that affinity could potentially have its own shorter retraining or recalculation cycle, without constantly changing the underlying storage strategy.

The warehouse could therefore maintain a relatively stable storage classification while allowing proximity recommendations to respond more dynamically to changes in actual order behavior.

Is This Already Being Done?

The concept of affinity-based or correlated slotting isn’t new in warehousing.

Similar principles are already used in areas such as market-basket analysis, warehouse optimization, and order-picking research.

What I am particularly curious about is the SAP EWM context.

Has anyone experimented with using order co-occurrence or association-rule analysis alongside standard EWM slotting?

For example, could this be explored through:

  • A custom BAdI
  • A side-by-side model on SAP BTP
  • HANA PAL
  • Custom analytics
  • A recommendation service
  • Or even a simpler analysis feeding recommendations back into the product or warehouse master data?

I would be very interested to hear how others have approached this.

Perhaps someone has already implemented a similar concept in an EWM environment, even if it wasn’t explicitly called “affinity-based slotting.”

Conclusion: From Smarter Products to Smarter Relationships

For me, the interesting part of this idea is not whether we can build another machine-learning model.

The technology to identify relationships between products already exists.

The more interesting question is whether we can use that intelligence in a way that complements the warehouse processes and controls already built into SAP EWM.

A product can be correctly classified based on its movement, physical characteristics, and storage requirements — and still be part of an inefficient picking journey because the products it frequently travels with are located far away.

That is where I see the potential of Smarter Neighbors.

The existing ML-based slotting logic could continue answering:

Where does this product belong?

An affinity layer could add another question:

Who should this product live next to?

Maybe the next step in intelligent slotting isn’t only teaching SAP EWM where a product belongs.

Maybe it’s also teaching the system which products belong together.

entry.title: What’s New in SAP HANA Cloud – September 2026
entry.content:
With the September 2026 release we are continuing to advance SAP HANA Cloud as an intelligent, AI-ready, and enterprise-scale data platform. This quarter introduces innovations that further enable agentic AI scenarios, bring AI closer to data modeling and development, strengthen business continuity, and simplify the management and optimization of enterprise workloads. 

From SAP Agent Memory Service and enhanced data discovery and retrieval capabilities, to AI-assisted Calculation View modeling, Knowledge Graph Engine innovations, and new performance and administration enhancements, this release makes it easier to build intelligent applications and work with enterprise data.

At the same time, new capabilities for multi-region disaster recovery, multitenancy, scalability, and SAP HANA Deployment Infrastructure (HDI) continue to strengthen SAP HANA Cloud as a secure and resilient foundation for business-critical workloads.

Whether you’re building agentic AI applications, simplifying data modeling and development, or optimizing and protecting your enterprise data landscape, SAP HANA Cloud continues to provide the foundation for intelligent, scalable, and resilient data management.

Let’s take a look at some of the key innovations introduced with the September 2026 release.

Agentic AI, Multi-Model & Knowledge Graph Innovations

Agent Memory Service for SAP HANA Cloud

AI agents that start every session from scratch cannot accumulate knowledge, recall past decisions, or carry user context forward. In QRC3 2026, we address this with the Agent Memory Service powered by SAP HANA Cloud: a managed API service built on SAP CAP that gives agents durable long-term memory and conversation history, backed by the SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine.

Memory entries are scoped by agentID and invokerID, keeping each agent-user pair isolated. The retrieval of past conversations and messages is semantic. Rather than flooding every prompt with an agent's full history, the /v1/memories/search endpoint uses SAP HANA Cloud's VECTOR_EMBEDDING and COSINE_SIMILARITY functions to surface only what is relevant to the current turn,  keeping prompts lean and inference costs low. Conversation messages are grouped via /v1/messages for replay and audit. Users retain full oversight, as memory entries can be inspected, edited, or deleted at any time.

Agents can now build on accumulated context across sessions, deliver progressively better outcomes, and do so entirely within the SAP HANA Cloud ecosystem.

AI_CORE_REQUEST — Call any AI Core Model Directly from SQL

Integrating large language models into data workflows has traditionally required application-layer middleware, handling external API calls, separate credential management, and data movement out of and back into the database. In QRC3 2026, AI_CORE_REQUEST removes that overhead entirely.

 

The new SQL function calls any AI Foundation Model registered in SAP AI Core directly from a SELECT statement, accepting a model name, a messages array, and optional inference parameters, and returning the model response as a structured result. AI enrichment, classification, and summarization become inline SQL operations with no external calls from the application tier. Binding AI_CORE_REQUEST to a generated column takes this further. Every insert or update can automatically trigger model inference, keeping AI-derived attributes continuously synchronized with the underlying data with zero additional application code required.

The result is AI-powered data pipelines that are architecturally simpler, easier to secure, and fully governed within the database.

GeoSPARQL Support in SAP HANA Cloud Knowledge Graph Engine

Spatial data - locations, boundaries, distances, routes - is core to logistics, asset management, environmental compliance, and supply chain operations. Until now, combining spatial reasoning with semantic graph queries required two separate engines and architectuarl approaches as well as two separate query languages. In QRC3 2026, the SAP HANA Cloud Knowledge Graph Engine adds GeoSPARQL support, closing that gap.

 

Geometry objects like points, line strings, polygons, can now be stored natively in RDF graphs using standard WKT literals, fully aligned with the OGC GeoSPARQL specification. Spatial functions including intersects, within, contains, distance, and overlaps work directly on graph data and compose naturally with semantic graph traversal in a single SPARQL query.
The implementation draws on SAP HANA Cloud's proven spatial engine, so geospatial predicates benefit from the same optimized indexing already used for SQL-based spatial workloads.

Data Exploration Tools — Expanded AI Model Support and Calculation View Discovery

The Data Exploration Tools in SAP HANA Cloud Central received two meaningful updates in QRC3 2026, making natural language database querying more flexible and more useful for analytics workloads.

First, the AI_OBJECT_RETRIEVAL and AI_DATA_RETRIEVAL procedures now support multiple large language models. The MODEL_AND_VERSION parameter accepts both gpt-4.1 (the default) and anthropic--claude-4.6-sonnet, and model selection is exposed directly in the SAP HANA Cloud Central UI when configuring a tool pair. Users choose their preferred model at setup, and that choice is passed to the underlying retrieval procedure at runtime, with no changes required to the SQL procedures themselves.

Second, Data Exploration Tools can now include Calculation Views alongside tables, views, and functions. Calculation Views are registered in the Knowledge Graph and RAG table, enabling the AI retrieval layer to discover them, understand their structure, and explain their purpose in response to natural language queries. This brings SAP HANA Cloud's analytic layer like cube models, dimension views, star joins  into reach of the same conversational interface already available for relational objects. CATALOG READ privilege is recommended for the dedicated database user to improve query performance, though the tool operates without it. 

AI-Assisted and Enhanced Calculation View Modeling

With Q3 2026, SAP HANA Cloud introduces a range of enhancements that make working with calculation views more intelligent and efficient. New AI-assisted capabilities help developers generate, explain, and optimize expressions using natural-language instructions, while calculation view metadata can now be published to a knowledge graph for AI-assisted discovery and retrieval. Additional modeling enhancements include Debug Mode to identify where specific records are lost, column impact analysis to understand how changes affect a model, dimension labels for clearer identification in analytics tools, and streamlined data preview and search experiences. Together, these updates simplify calculation view development, troubleshooting, and consumption across analytical and AI-driven scenarios.

To learn more please check this blogpost by @jan_zwickel 

Data Integration

SQL on Files: Apache Iceberg format version 3 support

Since QRC 3/2025, SAP HANA Cloud has enabled direct read-only access to Apache Iceberg tables in object storage, bringing real-time analytics to Iceberg lakehouses without moving data. That capability has continued to evolve, and with QRC 3/2026 it now extends to Apache Iceberg format version 3, keeping SAP HANA Cloud aligned with the latest open table format standard as the Iceberg ecosystem advances.

Format version 3 introduces binary deletion vectors, a more compact way to represent row-level deletes than the position delete files used in version 2. SAP HANA Cloud now reads format version 3 tables that adopt deletion vectors, preserving read correctness on these tables. Note that only the deletion vector capability of format version 3 is supported. Other version 3 features, including variant, geometry, geography, nanosecond-precision timestamps, column default values, and row-level lineage, are not supported. This selective adoption keeps behavior predictable while the broader ecosystem matures around the newer version 3 types.

Performance, Scalability & Administration

Analytics Advisor

Let’s start with an innovation designed to make performance optimization easier: the new Analytics Advisor.

For analytical workloads, identifying which queries are responsible for performance issues and determining the right optimization can require significant expertise and manual analysis.

The Analytics Advisor helps simplify this process by analyzing multidimensional query performance and identifying slow-running OLAP queries.

Partition Advisor

Staying with performance optimization, we’re also enhancing the Partition Advisor.

Until now, partitioning recommendations have primarily been based on the number of records within a partition. But row count alone doesn’t always provide the complete picture of how large a partition actually is.

With this release, the Partition Advisor can also take the actual memory size of partitions into account when generating recommendations.

This provides more accurate guidance and helps customers make better-informed partitioning decisions based on the real resource footprint of their data.

Support for additional 3 TB in the Memory Performance Class on AWS

A new intermediate memory performance instance class is now available on AWS, featuring 3 TB of memory and 185 vCPUs. This addition fills an important gap between the existing 1.8 TB—120 vCPU and 6 TB—440 vCPU instance sizes, providing a meaningful mid-tier option for customers whose workload requirements exceed the capabilities of smaller configurations but do not justify scaling to the largest available tier.

The new instance helps right-size infrastructure more effectively by avoiding the need to over-provision resources when additional memory capacity is required.  The 3 TB/185 vCPU instance introduces a more balanced alternative, enabling better alignment between workload demands and infrastructure sizing.

With a 1:16 memory-to-vCPU ratio, the instance is particularly well suited for SAP HANA Cloud workloads that require a strong balance of compute and memory resources. It provides additional CPU capacity for compute-intensive operations while maintaining a mid-range memory footprint making it an attractive option where scalability and cost efficiency are key considerations.

More details about the available options can be found SAP HANA Database Size. 

Business Continuity & Database Tenant Evolution

Supporting Multi-Region Disaster Recovery for Native Multitenancy

A regional outage shouldn't put your customers' data out of reach. With SAP HANA Cloud QRC3 we introduce a new Multi-Region Disaster Recovery capability for SAP HANA Cloud Multitenancy instances. It protects the database tenants of an SAP HANA database instance by replicating them, together with the database, to a secondary region.


The setup pairs two subaccounts in a BTP region pair, each with a database instance and a hana-multitenancy service instance. While the primary region is active, the secondary holds a passive replica that becomes operational only on failover. While replication is active, tenant data and metadata are continuously replicated asynchronously, meaning that the secondary handles no workload.

On failover, the secondary becomes the primay source. All tenants fail over together, and tenant metadata — IDs, access information, lifecycle changes, container references, and labels — is reconstructed so you can manage tenants via the Tenant Management Service REST API.

More information can be found in the SAP HANA Cloud online help.

Migrating Schemas and HDI Containers to SAP HANA Cloud Database Tenants

Already running your multi-tenant application on schemas or HDI containers? You can now transform them in place into full-fledged SAP HANA Cloud database tenants — and unlock tenant-level encryption, recovery, tenant move or copy, and workload isolation.

The migration is driven through the Tenant Management Service API and transforms an existing schema or HDI container into a database tenant within the same database instance. It runs asynchronously and is non-destructive: your original source container stays intact throughout.

Because it's non-destructive, migration is also low-risk. You can monitor progress until the tenant is ready, and if anything goes wrong, a rollback restores the original state. Once migration succeeds, you simply bind your application to the new database tenant and run it.

You can find more information in the SAP HANA Cloud online help.

Developer & SQL Experience

 

SQL Console

Query Data Visualization
The SQL Console now allows users to visualize query results as charts directly within the console, eliminating the need to export data or switch to a separate tool. After executing a query, users can seamlessly switch between the standard tabular view and a chart view. This enables quick visual analysis without leaving their workflow.

Supported chart types include Bar, Line, Pie, Donut, and Scatter charts. Users can configure chart axes using the columns returned by their query, providing flexibility in how data is represented and analyzed. This makes it easier to spot trends, compare values, and derive insights from query results at a glance.

Visual Indicator for Statement Results

When running multiple queries in the SQL Console, it can be easy to lose track of which result belongs to which statement. A new SQL toggle button in the results table header helps address this by displaying the executed SQL statement above its associated results tab. This makes the connection between the query and its output immediately clear.

Additionally, when enabled through user settings, navigating between results tabs automatically highlights the corresponding SQL statement in the editor, making it even easier to trace results back to their source without manual searching.

Fixed-Width Font Option

Users can now switch the SQL results view to a fixed-width (monospace) font, providing improved alignment and readability for query output. This is particularly useful when working with formatted text output or structured data, where consistent character spacing helps preserve structure and visual clarity.

Fixed-Width Font Enabled:

Fixed-Width Font Disabled:

The font option can be toggled to suit individual preferences, allowing users to work in the format that best fits their workflow. By improving the presentation of query results, this enhancement makes it easier to review output, compare values, and interpret formatted data directly within the SQL Console.

 

SAP HANA HDI updates

Simplified HDI API for Build Plugins. SAP HANA Cloud now offers a simplified API for writing custom HDI build plugins, cutting down the boilerplate needed to build and maintain deployment logic for design-time artifacts. See the Simple HDI API reference for details.

Smarter Index Redeployment. Indexes are currently redeployed via a full drop and recreate, which gets expensive when multiple indexes are involved. The new redeploy support lets the index plugin update indexes in place instead. Since the table plugin runs first and drops all indexes to make its own comparison work, the index plugin needs to handle the case where an index is already missing and simply recreate it. For the optimization to pay off end-to-end, the table data plugin also needs to skip redeploying data when its CSV file hasn't changed.

SAP HANA Tools MCP Server. SAP has shipped the SAP HANA Tools MCP Server (@sap/hana-tooling-mcp-server), giving AI coding assistants live, verifiable access to your HANA instance and HDI projects via the Model Context Protocol, SQL validation and execution, schema-aware documentation search, HDI artifact scaffolding, and deploy/recover/status tools, with credentials handled securely and executeSql disabled by default. Details in the SAP HANA Tools MCP Server documentation.

 

Expanded Availability on SAP Sovereign Cloud 

As part of our continued investment in SAP Sovereign Cloud, we’re expanding the availability of SAP HANA Cloud to meet growing customer demand for digital sovereignty.

In the Q3 2026 timeframe, we delivered two key updates:

First, SAP HANA Cloud is now available in two new SAP Sovereign Cloud regions: India, deployed on AWS, and Europe/Germany, deployed on SAP Cloud Infrastructure. The Europe/Germany availability is particularly significant for regulated European customers. It is an SAP Sovereign Cloud deployment where SAP delivers sovereignty across the full stack on SAP-owned hardware located in Germany.

Second, SAP HANA Cloud at SAP NS2 has received FedRAMP certification. This makes the offering ready for adoption by U.S. federal civilian agencies for their regulated workloads.

Together, these updates allow more highly regulated organizations to adopt SAP HANA Cloud while meeting stringent compliance and regulatory requirements. Learn more in this blogpost by @isomesan 

 

 

Thanks for taking the time to explore the What’s New in SAP HANA Cloud on Q3 2026 innovations!

If you’d like to go deeper into the technical details of the September 2026 release, we recommend visiting the What’s New Viewer in the technical documentation. It provides a comprehensive overview of the full release scope. To stay informed about upcoming innovations, announcements, and best practices, follow the SAP HANA Cloud tag.

You can also find our latest blog posts by searching for the #whatsnewinsaphanacloud hashtag.

If you missed earlier What’s New webinars, you’ll find recordings of past sessions and upcoming events in our YouTube playlist. Our What’s New webinar covering the Q3 2026 innovations will be posted on this playlist very soon.

We’d love to hear from you!

entry.title: Calculation View Features of 2026 QRC3
entry.content:
Within the time frame of 2026 Q3, several new calculation view features have been released in SAP Business Application Studio when connected to SAP HANA Cloud database QRC3. Some of these features are highlighted below. You can find examples that illustrate the individual features here. An overview of features of other releases can be found here.

Generate Expressions Leveraging AI support

To generate expressions in calculated columns, restricted columns or filter expressions,  describe your intend in natural language as a comment in the expression editor:

-- calculate the final prices with 10 percent discount for products with status "Clearance" and 10 percent on top for products with status is "Best Seller"

Use the AI option "Generate Expression with AI" to generate the corresponding statement. The AI decision will be based on the available column names in the current node and your comment:

Similarly you can mark your expression and choose "Explain Expression with AI" to better understand an existing expression:

Or you can use AI support to "Optimize Expression with AI", e.g. to remove redundant checks or calculations.

Leverage AI to simplify creating expressions and to optimize expressions

Investigate Why Specific Records are Missing in the Result

Use Debug Mode to pinpoint exactly where a specific record disappears within a calculation view.

When you specify a column value to investigate, Debug Mode let's you trigger queries against each node in the model. The result shows how often that record is returned at each node, letting you quickly identify the node where it drops out - and focus your analysis there.
 
While value “1001” is present after node “CompleteData” it is missing after node “Filter1001”

 

Note: Trace queries run against every node in the model. Execution time scales with model complexity and query scope.

Use Debug Mode to quickly identify where a record gets lost

Column Impact Within Model

Column lineage allows to trace the sources of a column. In contrast, to find out where a column is used in the current calculation view, use Show Impact in the Mapping pane:

This will display the impacted columns within the current calculation view.

Use column impact information to understand the impact a change of a column would have.

Simplified Copying of Calculation View ID

The calculation view ID determines the name of the calculation view object that is created in the database. To simplify copying it, it is now displayed at the top of the modeling screen.

Clicking into the box automatically copies the calculation view ID:

A dedicated option to copy the calculation view ID is also available in the modelling section of the context menu of a calculation view:

Use the option to quickly copy the calculation view ID without the need to open the calculation view editor

 

Label Dimensions

Add Alias Name and Alias Label for dimensions in star joins to more easily identify them in analytics tools such as SAP Analytics Cloud:

 

Afterwards, the Alias Label will become available in e.g., SAP Analytics Cloud:

Multi language is supported using properties files.

If multiple dimensions have the same source, define alias names for dimensions to distinguish between them in reporting tools such as SAP Analytics Cloud

 

Open New SQL Console for Data Preview

Each Data Preview now opens in a dedicated SQL console by default. This preserves your previous results and any SQL modifications, making it easier to compare outputs across multiple previews.

To revert to the previous behavior - where all previews share a single console - select option "Reuse Existing Console" under: [Settings > wattFeature > calculationViewEditor > dataPreview]

 

The first time you open a Data Preview in your developer workspace with the new behavior, you will be prompted to choose your preferred behavior.

Open a new SQL console for each Data Preview to compare results and retain SQL modifications across sessions.

 

Find Data Sources with Exact Matches


When searching for data sources in calculation views or analytic privileges, you can switch between two search modes: Contains and Exact Match.

Contains returns any object whose name includes the search string, regardless of position which is the Default mode
Exact Match matches the full object name and supports SQL wildcards: _ (single character) and % (any characters)
 
Example: Searching "sales%" in Exact Match mode returns objects whose names start with "sales" - but excludes objects where "sales" appears mid-name, such as "YTD_salesOrder":
 

 

 
The last selection is remembered per workspace.
 
Exact Match Mode is required for Analytic Privilege Wildcard Patterns:

entry.title: Unlocking Currency Conversion in SQLScript with CONVERT_CURRENCY() in SAP HANA XSA and Datasphere
entry.content:
Currency conversion is a common requirement in SAP reporting, analytics, pricing, and planning scenarios. Whether you are developing SQLScript Table Functions in SAP HANA XSA, building reusable data models in SAP HANA Cloud, or creating analytical models in SAP Datasphere, you will eventually need to compare and report data maintained in multiple currencies.

SAP provides the built-in CONVERT_CURRENCY() function to perform currency conversion directly within SQL. Rather than implementing custom exchange rate logic, developers can leverage SAP's standard currency conversion framework and exchange rate tables.

This article provides a practical overview of how to use CONVERT_CURRENCY() in SAP HANA XSA and SAP Datasphere, along with some implementation patterns that I've found useful in real-world projects.

If You Have Already Used Currency Conversion in Calculation Views...

If you've previously configured Currency Conversion for a measure within the Semantics node of a HANA Calculation View, many of the concepts used by CONVERT_CURRENCY() will already be familiar.

Both approaches rely on the same fundamental business concepts:

  • Amount
  • Source Currency
  • Target Currency
  • Exchange Rate Type
  • Reference Date

The primary difference is that Calculation Views expose these settings through a graphical interface, whereas CONVERT_CURRENCY() provides direct access through SQLScript.

Basic Syntax

CONVERT_CURRENCY(
    "AMOUNT" => NET_VALUE,
    "SOURCE_UNIT" => SALES_CURRENCY,
    "TARGET_UNIT" => 'USD',
    "REFERENCE_DATE" => CURRENT_DATE,
    "CLIENT" => '500',
    "SCHEMA" => 'MY_SCHEMA'
)

The function converts the amount from the source currency into the target currency using the exchange rate configuration defined in the SAP currency conversion framework.

Most Common Parameters

Although the function supports a large number of parameters, most implementations typically use the following:

  • AMOUNT – Monetary value to be converted
  • SOURCE_UNIT – Source currency
  • TARGET_UNIT – Reporting currency
  • REFERENCE_DATE – Date used to determine the exchange rate
  • CONVERSION_TYPE – Exchange rate type (for example M, P, or B)
  • ERROR_HANDLING – Controls behavior when exchange rates cannot be determined

Additional parameters are available for specifying the underlying currency conversion tables, which is especially relevant for HDI Container-based implementations.

Using CONVERT_CURRENCY() in SAP HANA XSA

One practical use case involved reporting SAP pricing conditions in a common currency. Pricing records were maintained globally using multiple currencies, but the business required global reporting in USD.

The following example converts a pricing condition value into USD:

CONVERT_CURRENCY(
    "AMOUNT" => "KBETR",
    "SOURCE_UNIT" => "KONWA",
    "TARGET_UNIT" => 'USD',
    "CLIENT" => '500',
    "SCHEMA" => 'MY_HDI_SCHEMA',
    "REFERENCE_DATE" => CURRENT_DATE,
    "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'P',
    "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null'
) AS "KBETR_USD"

This provides a standardized price regardless of the original currency in which the pricing condition was maintained.

Working with HDI Containers

Many SAP HANA XSA projects expose SAP currency tables through synonyms rather than directly accessing the underlying TCUR* tables.

Typical examples include:

TCURR_CV_SYN
TCURF_CV_SYN
TCURV_CV_SYN
TCURN_CV_SYN
TCURX_CV_SYN

In these scenarios, the synonym objects can be passed directly into CONVERT_CURRENCY():

CONVERT_CURRENCY(
    "AMOUNT" => "KBETR",
    "SOURCE_UNIT" => "KONWA",
    "TARGET_UNIT" => 'USD',
    "CLIENT" => '500',
    "SCHEMA" => 'MY_HDI_SCHEMA',
    "REFERENCE_DATE" => CURRENT_DATE,
    "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'P',
    "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null',
    "CONFIGURATION_TABLE" => 'TCURV_CV_SYN',
    "PRECISIONS_TABLE" => 'TCURX_CV_SYN',
    "NOTATIONS_TABLE" => 'TCURN_CV_SYN',
    "RATES_TABLE" => 'TCURR_CV_SYN',
    "PREFACTORS_TABLE" => 'TCURF_CV_SYN'
)

This is a common pattern in HDI Container-based applications where SAP ERP or S/4HANA metadata is exposed through synonyms.

Combining Unit Conversion and Currency Conversion

In many pricing scenarios, comparing currencies alone is not sufficient. Prices may also be maintained using different pricing units or units of measure.

In one implementation, the pricing condition was first normalized into a common reporting unit:

K."KBETR" * (UN."UMREZ" / UN."UMREN")

The normalized value was then converted into USD:

CONVERT_CURRENCY(
    "AMOUNT" => K."KBETR" * (UN."UMREZ" / UN."UMREN"),
    "SOURCE_UNIT" => K."KONWA",
    "TARGET_UNIT" => 'USD',
    "CLIENT" => '500',
    "SCHEMA" => 'MY_HDI_SCHEMA',
    "REFERENCE_DATE" => CURRENT_DATE,
    "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'P',
    "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null'
)

This produces pricing values that are comparable across:

  • Multiple currencies
  • Different pricing units
  • Different units of measure

Using CONVERT_CURRENCY() in SAP Datasphere SQL Views

CONVERT_CURRENCY() is not limited to SAP HANA XSA. Developers working with SAP Datasphere can also use the function directly within SQL Views running in SQLScript mode.

For example:

CONVERT_CURRENCY(
    "AMOUNT" => "GROSS_SALES_VALUE",
    "SOURCE_UNIT" => "SALES_CURRENCY",
    "TARGET_UNIT" => 'USD',
    "REFERENCE_DATE" => "SALES_DATE",
    "CLIENT" => '100',
    "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'M',
    "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null'
)

This approach provides full flexibility for implementing custom currency conversion logic directly inside Datasphere SQL models.

Using CONVERT_CURRENCY() in Datasphere Graphical Views

One capability that is easy to overlook is that developers are not limited to using CONVERT_CURRENCY() within SQL Views. SAP Datasphere also allows the function to be embedded directly within Calculated Columns in Graphical Views.

For example:

CONVERT_CURRENCY(
    "AMOUNT" => "GROSS_SALES_VALUE",
    "SOURCE_UNIT" => "SALES_CURRENCY",
    "TARGET_UNIT" => :P_REPORTING_CURRENCY,
    "REFERENCE_DATE" => :P_EXCHANGE_RATE_DATE,
    "CLIENT" => '500',
    "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'M',
    "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null'
)

This combines the simplicity of graphical modelling with the flexibility of parameter-driven currency conversion. Business users can dynamically choose reporting currencies and exchange-rate dates without modifying the model itself.

Making Currency Conversion Dynamic

Hardcoding target currencies and dates may be suitable for some reporting scenarios, but many business users require flexibility.

By utilizing input parameters, the same logic can support multiple reporting currencies:

CONVERT_CURRENCY(
    "AMOUNT" => "NET_REVENUE",
    "SOURCE_UNIT" => "DOCUMENT_CURRENCY",
    "TARGET_UNIT" => :P_TARGET_CURRENCY,
    "REFERENCE_DATE" => :P_RATE_DATE,
    "CONVERSION_TYPE" => 'M',
    "ERROR_HANDLING" => 'set to null'
)

This pattern works particularly well in SAP Datasphere analytical models and parameter-driven reporting scenarios.

Conclusion

CONVERT_CURRENCY() is a useful built-in function available across SAP HANA XSA, SAP HANA Cloud, and SAP Datasphere. Whether you're building SQLScript Table Functions, SQL Views, or Graphical Views, the function provides a consistent and flexible way to perform currency conversion using SAP's standard currency conversion framework.

By understanding the core parameters, HDI Container considerations, and Datasphere integration options, developers can significantly reduce the effort required to implement robust currency conversion logic across enterprise reporting and analytical solutions.

References

  • SAP HANA Cloud SQL Reference Guide - CONVERT_CURRENCY Function
  • SAP SQLScript Currency Conversion Example

Introduction

In many retail and distribution businesses, a customer order is created with a single shipping location, but the goods must be delivered to multiple store locations. Although the sales order and outbound delivery are created from a common shipping point, warehouse execution requires store-specific picking logic.

A recent business requirement involved ensuring that:

  • One Sales Order contains multiple Store Locations.
  • During EWM Outbound Delivery Order (ODO) creation, the Warehouse Process Type (WPT) must be determined based on the Store Location.
  • Warehouse Tasks (WTs) belonging to the same store should be assigned to the same warehouse operator.
  • Multiple WTs should be combined into a single Warehouse Order (WO) through Warehouse Order Creation Rules (WOCR).
  • Standard WPT determination was insufficient because store information was not part of the standard determination criteria.

To address this requirement, a custom enhancement was implemented using BADI /SCWM/EX_DLV_DET_PROCTYPE, method CHANGE_PROCTYPE, which SAP provides for modifying the Warehouse Process Type determined during delivery processing. The BADI can be used to change the warehouse process type after SAP's standard determination logic has executed.

Business Scenario

Existing Process

  1. Sales Order is created in SAP S/4HANA.
  2. Outbound Delivery is generated.
  3. Delivery is distributed to SAP EWM.
  4. EWM creates the Outbound Delivery Order (ODO).
  5. Standard WPT determination occurs.
  6. Warehouse Tasks are created.

Challenge

  • Warehouse Tasks being split across different WOCR strategies.
  • Multiple Warehouse Orders being created.
  • Different users receiving tasks for the same shipment.
  • Reduced warehouse productivity and increased travel distance.

The business required store-specific WPT determination so that downstream WOCR logic could consolidate Warehouse Tasks into a single executable Warehouse Order.

entry.title: CDS Table Functions: does your WHERE really reach the table? (measured)
entry.content:
Every abstraction layer is a promise. A CDS Table Function promises that you can write SQLScript and still consume the result like any other CDS entity: with a WHERE, with a view on top, from RAP, from ABAP SQL. Promises tend to decay quietly, so I decided to check this one.

The question

You put WHERE region = '07' on top of your CDS Table Function. Does HANA apply that filter at the table, or does it run your whole function and throw away 95% of the rows at the end?

Most of us answer this from memory ("table functions are a black box", or "HANA inlines everything now"). I wanted numbers and execution plans, so I built a small lab and measured it.

The setup

  • System: S/4HANA 2023, SAP_BASIS 758 SP01, HANA 2.00.073 (lab system).
  • Data: table ZTF_SALES with 2,000,000 rows in one client, 20 regions with 100,000 rows each. Every test filters region 07, which is 5% of the data.
  • Four table functions with the same output and the same AMDP class, changing only the SQLScript style:
    • TF_A: declarative, a single RETURN SELECT.
    • TF_B: multi-step, intermediate table variables.
    • TF_C: imperative, a scalar SELECT ... INTO followed by an IF before the final SELECT.
    • TF_D: the region passed as an input parameter and applied inside the SQLScript.
  • Plus a CDS view entity on top of TF_A, a very common pattern in real projects.
  • Method: 1 warm-up and 10 runs per case with GET RUN TIME (average shown), execution plans from EXPLAIN PLAN via ADBC, database time from the HANA SQL plan cache.

The results

SourceFetch rows, region 07COUNT, region 07COUNT, no filterWhere the filter appears in the plan
Table (direct)32.8 ms1.0 ms1.1 msTABLE SCAN ZTF_SALES
TF_A declarative35.2 ms1.8 ms1.7 msIn the table scan; the function disappears from the plan
TF_B multi-step38.4 ms2.4 ms1.5 msIn the table scan; lt1/lt2 are dissolved
TF_C imperative283.5 ms246.3 ms244.8 msFILTER above TABLE FUNCTION GET_C
TF_D with p_region35.8 ms2.4 msn/aIn the table scan (REGION = ?1)
View on top of TF_A42.3 ms2.5 ms2.1 msIn the table scan; the filter crosses the view and the function

Fetch times include transferring 100,000 rows to ABAP. In pure database time (plan cache), TF_A took 22.5 ms against 21.5 ms for the direct table, while TF_C took 272.8 ms.

What the plans show

Simplified excerpts from EXPLAIN PLAN.

TF_A (TF_B and the view look the same): the function is gone, the outer WHERE sits on the table scan.

PROJECT                         est. 119,180 rows
  TABLE SCAN ZTF_SALES          filter: CLIENT = ?  AND  REGION = '07'

TF_D: the parameter lands in the same place.

TABLE SCAN ZTF_SALES            filter: ... AND REGION = ?1

View on top of TF_A: the filter crosses two layers and still reaches the scan.

TABLE SCAN ZTF_SALES            filter: CLIENT = SESSION_CONTEXT('CDS_CLIENT')
                                    AND CLIENT = SESSION_CONTEXT('CLIENT')
                                    AND REGION = '07'

TF_C: the function stays in the plan as a box, and the region filter is applied on its result.

PROJECT                                   est. 10 rows
  FILTER  ZTF_SALES_C.REGION = '07'
    TABLE FUNCTION ZCL_TF_SALES=>GET_C      est. 10,000 rows
      (parameter P_CLNT)

Inside TF_C, the plan cache shows the final SELECT of the procedure filtered by client only. The region never reaches it, so the function produces the whole client (this part is a deduction from the plan, not a row count I measured). The outer filter saves nothing: TF_C takes about 245 ms with or without it.

Takeaways

  1. Declarative table functions are inlined. On this release, a single RETURN SELECT or a chain of table variables is merged into the calling statement. The outer WHERE reaches the table scan, and the cost is close to reading the table directly.
  2. Imperative logic blocks it. One scalar SELECT ... INTO plus an IF was enough to turn the function into a black box: about 8x slower fetching the rows and more than 100x slower on the COUNT, because the filter is applied after the function has produced everything.
  3. The input parameter did not beat TF_A, because TF_A was already inlined. My inference (not measured here): passing the filter as a parameter pays off when the function contains logic that blocks inlining. If you need imperative steps, take the selective filters as parameters and apply them in the first SELECT.

Bonus: client handling

  • On 758, a client-dependent table function with @ClientHandling.algorithm: #SESSION_VARIABLE requires a client parameter annotated with @Environment.systemField: #CLIENT; without it activation fails with SDDL_PARSER_MSG 157. A view on top must pass p_clnt: $session.client.
  • I also built a variant without the client condition inside the SQLScript and added 20,000 rows in a second client. Through ABAP SQL, the result contained only the logon client, because ABAP SQL adds its own client condition. Called directly on the database via ADBC, the same function also returned the rows of the other client. The protection is ABAP SQL, not your function, so keep the client filter inside the SQLScript.

The code

Table:

@AbapCatalog.deliveryClass : #A
define table ztf_sales {
  key client : abap.clnt not null;
  key id     : abap.int4 not null;
  region     : abap.char(2);
  matnr      : abap.char(18);
  @Semantics.amount.currencyCode : 'ztf_sales.currency'
  amount     : abap.curr(15,2);
  currency   : abap.cuky;
  sdate      : abap.dats;
}

Table function (TF_A):

@EndUserText.label: 'Sales - declarative table function'
@ClientHandling.type: #CLIENT_DEPENDENT
@ClientHandling.algorithm: #SESSION_VARIABLE
define table function ZTF_SALES_A
  with parameters
    @Environment.systemField: #CLIENT
    p_clnt : abap.clnt
  returns {
    client : abap.clnt;
    region : abap.char(2);
    matnr  : abap.char(18);
    amount : abap.dec(15,2);
    sdate  : abap.dats;
  }
  implemented by method zcl_tf_sales=>get_a;

" ZTF_SALES_B and ZTF_SALES_C are identical except for name and method.
" ZTF_SALES_D adds a second parameter:  p_region : abap.char(2)

Consumption view:

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Consumption view on top of ZTF_SALES_A'
define view entity ZI_TF_SALES_A
  as select from ZTF_SALES_A( p_clnt: $session.client )
{
  region,
  matnr,
  amount,
  sdate
}

AMDP class, method bodies:

" All methods: BY DATABASE FUNCTION FOR HDB LANGUAGE SQLSCRIPT
"              OPTIONS READ-ONLY USING ztf_sales

METHOD get_a.            " declarative, single RETURN SELECT
  RETURN SELECT client, region, matnr, amount, sdate
           FROM ztf_sales
          WHERE client = SESSION_CONTEXT('CLIENT');
ENDMETHOD.

METHOD get_b.            " multi-step, table variables
  lt1 = SELECT client, region, matnr, amount, sdate
          FROM ztf_sales
         WHERE client = SESSION_CONTEXT('CLIENT');
  lt2 = SELECT client, region, matnr, amount, sdate FROM :lt1;
  RETURN :lt2;
ENDMETHOD.

METHOD get_c.            " imperative: scalar SELECT INTO + IF
  DECLARE lv_cnt   INTEGER;
  DECLARE lv_limit NVARCHAR(8) := '99991231';
  SELECT COUNT(*) INTO lv_cnt
    FROM ztf_sales
   WHERE client = SESSION_CONTEXT('CLIENT') AND id = 1;
  IF :lv_cnt = 0 THEN
    lv_limit := '00000000';
  END IF;
  RETURN SELECT client, region, matnr, amount, sdate
           FROM ztf_sales
          WHERE client = SESSION_CONTEXT('CLIENT')
            AND sdate <= :lv_limit;
ENDMETHOD.

METHOD get_d.            " filter as input parameter
  RETURN SELECT client, region, matnr, amount, sdate
           FROM ztf_sales
          WHERE client = SESSION_CONTEXT('CLIENT')
            AND region = :p_region;
ENDMETHOD.

Caveats

  • One system, one release, uniformly distributed data, in a shared lab. HANA Cloud and the BTP ABAP Environment may behave differently.
  • Row counts in the plans are optimizer estimates. I did not use PlanViz, so I have no measured "rows read" figure.
  • TF_C is one way to block inlining. Cursors, loops and SEQUENTIAL EXECUTION were not tested.

Your turn

Have you seen a declarative table function that was not inlined, or other SQLScript constructs that keep the filter out? I would like to compare notes, especially on HANA Cloud.

Measurements were run in my own lab with my MCP tooling against the SAP system. The text was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by me.
