entry.title: CDS joins you don't read: does HANA really skip them? (measured)
entry.content:
In my last post I checked if a WHERE on top of a CDS table function really reaches the table. This one goes the other way. Your view has three joins, and the consumer reads only one or two fields. Does HANA still execute all the joins?

Most of us answer this from memory: "HANA prunes unused joins", or "only with associations", or "only if you declare the cardinality". I wanted to see the plans, so I built a small lab on two releases.

The question

A view joins MARA with MAKT (texts) and T134 (material types). A report selects only the material number. Which joins does HANA really execute? And what happens to the result when the cardinality you declared is not true?

The setup

  • Systems: S/4HANA 2023 (SAP_BASIS 758, HANA 2.00.073) and S/4HANA 2020 (SAP_BASIS 755, HANA 2.00.052), both lab systems.
  • Data: the standard tables with the demo data that was already there. 2023: 1,199 materials and 2,051 material texts in 3 languages. 2020: 2,566 materials and 19,885 material texts in many languages.
  • Eight CDS view entities on MARA, changing only how the join is written:
  • ZJP_OUTER: LEFT OUTER JOIN to MAKT (language 'E' in the ON condition) and to T134, no cardinality.
  • ZJP_TOONE: the same with LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN.
  • ZJP_ASSOC: the same with association [0..1] and a path in the field list.
  • ZJP_INNER: INNER JOIN to T134.
  • ZJP_VIEW_OUTER: LEFT OUTER JOIN to a view entity on T134 instead of the table (VDM style), no cardinality.
  • ZJP_VIEW_TOONE: the same with LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN.
  • ZJP_TEXT: LEFT OUTER JOIN to MAKT without the language, no cardinality. One row per material and language, and the view says so.
  • ZJP_TEXT_ONE: association [0..1] to MAKT without the language. This cardinality is a lie: a material has one text per language.
  • Three consumer statements per view, in ABAP SQL: only Material, Material plus one joined field, and COUNT(*).
  • Method: rows counted in ABAP. For the plans I looked up the statement that ABAP SQL really sent in the HANA SQL plan cache and ran EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SQL PLAN CACHE ENTRY via ADBC. So each plan belongs to the real ABAP statement, not to a native SQL I typed by hand.

The results

Both releases gave the same plans. Rows are shown as 2023 / 2020.

ViewOnly MaterialMaterial + joined fieldCOUNT(*)Tables in the plan, only Material
ZJP_OUTER, no cardinality1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_TOONE, to one1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_ASSOC, [0..1]1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_VIEW_OUTER, join to a view1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_VIEW_TOONE1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_INNER1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA, T134
ZJP_TEXT, no language, no cardinality2,051 / 19,8852,051 / 19,8852,051 / 19,885MARA, MAKT
ZJP_TEXT_ONE, no language, [0..1]1,199 / 2,5662,051 / 19,8851,199 / 2,566MARA

The COUNT(*) plans follow the same pattern: MARA alone, except ZJP_INNER and ZJP_TEXT. With Material plus the text, ZJP_OUTER joins MAKT and still leaves T134 out.

Look at the last line. Same view, same WHERE (none), and the number of rows depends on the fields the consumer selects.

What the plans show

Simplified excerpts from the 2023 system. The 2020 system shows COLUMN SEARCH on MARA instead of TABLE SCAN, with the same tables.

ZJP_OUTER, only Material. Both joins are gone:

SELECT /* FDA READ */ "MATERIAL" FROM "ZJP_OUTER" WHERE "MANDT" = ?

PROJECT
  TABLE SCAN MARA

ZJP_OUTER, Material and text. MAKT comes back, T134 stays out:

COLUMN SEARCH
  JOIN
    COLUMN TABLE MARA
    COLUMN TABLE MAKT

ZJP_INNER, only Material. The join stays, because an inner join can remove rows:

COLUMN SEARCH
  JOIN
    COLUMN TABLE MARA
    COLUMN TABLE T134

ZJP_TEXT_ONE: with only Material, HANA reads MARA alone and returns 2,566 rows on 2020. Add the text and the join comes back with 19,885 rows, about 7.7 times more.

Where the cardinality goes

The SQL that activation generates for each view (ADT shows it) was the same on both releases:

  • LEFT OUTER JOIN without cardinality stays LEFT OUTER JOIN.
  • LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN and association [0..1] both become LEFT OUTER MANY TO ONE JOIN.
  • ZJP_TEXT_ONE also becomes LEFT OUTER MANY TO ONE JOIN, with only MANDT and MATNR in the ON condition. HANA has no way to know that this is false, so it trusts it.

Does anyone warn you?

  • 2023, association [0..1] without the language: activation passes with warning DD_CDS_ANALYSIS 302, "Cardinality 1 of Association _TEXT does not match to the ON-condition".
  • 2023, the same mistake written as LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN: no cardinality warning in the syntax check.
  • 2020: no warning for either version. The message text exists in the 2020 system, but the check did not fire for this view.

So the only warning I got was on the newer release, only for the association, and it is a warning: the view activates and runs.

Takeaways

  • HANA drops a LEFT OUTER JOIN you don't read when it can prove the join returns at most one row. Here it got that proof in two ways: the ON condition covered the whole primary key of the joined table (ZJP_OUTER needed no cardinality at all), or I declared it (TO ONE or [0..1]). A simple view entity in between did not stop it. My reading is that HANA used the primary keys of MAKT and T134; I did not test a join that is unique in the data but not by key.
  • An INNER JOIN is never dropped, even when you read nothing from it, because it can remove rows. If the lookup is optional, LEFT OUTER is not only the right semantics, it also lets HANA skip it.
  • When HANA cannot prove "to one" (ZJP_TEXT), it keeps the join. That is the safe default.
  • When you declare "to one" and it is not true, HANA believes you. The row count then depends on which fields the consumer selects: a list with the text shows 19,885 lines, the COUNT(*) on the same view says 2,566. For text associations, put the language in the ON condition (usually $session.system_language).

About time: with these small tables, the difference between a dropped and a kept join was below 1 ms per query and inside the noise of 10 runs, so I am not using time as the argument here. The gain grows with the size of the dropped tables, which I did not measure. The lie was visible in time on 2020: 3.7 ms for the 2,566 rows against 66.7 ms for the 19,885 rows (average of 10 runs with GET RUN TIME, including the transfer to ABAP).

The code

Views, with the annotations removed:

define view entity ZJP_OUTER
  as select from mara
    left outer join makt on  makt.matnr = mara.matnr
                         and makt.spras = 'E'
    left outer join t134 on t134.mtart = mara.mtart
{
  key mara.matnr as Material,
      mara.mtart as MaterialType,
      makt.maktx as MaterialText,
      t134.mtref as ReferenceType
}

// ZJP_TOONE: the same, with "left outer to one join" in both joins.

define view entity ZJP_ASSOC
  as select from mara
  association [0..1] to makt as _Text on  _Text.matnr = $projection.Material
                                      and _Text.spras = 'E'
  association [0..1] to t134 as _Type on _Type.mtart = $projection.MaterialType
{
  key mara.matnr  as Material,
      mara.mtart  as MaterialType,
      _Text.maktx as MaterialText,
      _Type.mtref as ReferenceType
}

define view entity ZJP_INNER
  as select from mara
    inner join t134 on t134.mtart = mara.mtart
{
  key mara.matnr as Material,
      mara.mtart as MaterialType,
      t134.mtref as ReferenceType
}

define view entity ZJP_TYPE
  as select from t134
{
  key mtart as MaterialType,
      mtref as ReferenceType
}

define view entity ZJP_VIEW_OUTER
  as select from mara
    left outer join ZJP_TYPE as Typ on Typ.MaterialType = mara.mtart
{
  key mara.matnr        as Material,
      mara.mtart        as MaterialType,
      Typ.ReferenceType as ReferenceType
}

// ZJP_VIEW_TOONE: the same, with "left outer to one join".

define view entity ZJP_TEXT
  as select from mara
    left outer join makt on makt.matnr = mara.matnr
{
  key mara.matnr as Material,
  key makt.spras as Language,
      mara.mtart as MaterialType,
      makt.maktx as MaterialText
}

define view entity ZJP_TEXT_ONE        // the lie: no language in the ON condition
  as select from mara
  association [0..1] to makt as _Text on _Text.matnr = $projection.Material
{
  key mara.matnr  as Material,
      mara.mtart  as MaterialType,
      _Text.maktx as MaterialText
}

How I read the plan of the real ABAP statement:

SELECT material FROM zjp_outer INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_rows).   " the consumer

" ADBC: find the statement in the plan cache and explain the cached plan
DATA(lo_st) = cl_sql_connection=>get_connection( )->create_statement( ).
" SELECT PLAN_ID FROM M_SQL_PLAN_CACHE
"  WHERE STATEMENT_STRING LIKE '%"ZJP_OUTER"%'
lo_st->execute_update( |EXPLAIN PLAN SET STATEMENT_NAME = 'JP1'| &&
                       | FOR SQL PLAN CACHE ENTRY { lv_plan_id }| ).
" SELECT OPERATOR_NAME, TABLE_NAME FROM EXPLAIN_PLAN_TABLE
"  WHERE STATEMENT_NAME = 'JP1'

Caveats

  • Two releases, lab systems, small demo data, one client each. I could not reach a 2025 system (SAP_BASIS 816) for this round.
  • Simple joins only. The view on the right side was a plain projection. VDM views with unions, aggregations or their own joins on the right side were not tested.
  • The LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN version of the lie was only syntax checked, not activated and run. That syntax generates the same MANY TO ONE join (see ZJP_TOONE), so I expect the same behavior, but I did not measure it.
  • Plans come from EXPLAIN PLAN (the optimizer). I did not use PlanViz.
  • HANA Cloud and the BTP ABAP Environment were not tested.

Your turn

Have you seen a "to one" join that HANA did not drop? Or a KPI that did not match the list behind it because of a cardinality? I would like to compare notes, especially on 2025 and on HANA Cloud.

entry.title: SAP HANA Data Provisioning Agent 2.8.1.2 on SLES 15.6 Installation and Connection to SAP HANA Cloud
entry.content:
The SAP HANA Data Provisioning Agent (DP Agent) is the on-premise component of SAP HANA smart data integration (SDI). It lets SAP HANA Cloud reach data sources inside your own network, for example to create virtual tables.

In this guide I install the DP Agent on SLES 15 SP6 and connect its configuration tool to an SAP HANA Cloud database. Registering the agent is not covered, for the reason explained at the end.

Lab environment

  • SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 15 SP6 (VM)
  • SAP HANA Data Provisioning Agent 2.8.1.2, Linux x86_64
  • SAP HANA Cloud free tier instance in an SAP BTP trial account

Step 1 – Create the SAP HANA Cloud instance

In the SAP BTP cockpit, open Service Marketplace, search for hana and choose SAP HANA Cloud .

 

Create an instance with the plan hana-free, runtime Cloud Foundry and a name of your choice.

In the Parameters step I set memory, systempassword and edition. The system password is the one used for DBADMIN later.

 

In my lab the name is hdb. Wait until the instance status is Usable.

 

 

Step 2 – Subscribe to SAP HANA Cloud tools

SAP HANA Cloud Central needs its own subscription. Without it you see No subscription.

 

Subscribe to SAP HANA Cloud with the plan tools, then choose Go to Application.

 

Step 3 – Assign the role collections

Without the SAP HANA Cloud role collections, SAP HANA Cloud Central answers Not authorized.

 

.In the cockpit open Security, Users, select your user and choose Assign Role Collection .

 

Sign out and sign in again afterwards.

Step 4 – Register the instance and prepare access

The instance now appears in SAP HANA Cloud Central as Running, Free tier.

 

Register it with the DBADMIN user.

Copy the SQL endpoint of the instance (Actions, Copy SQL Endpoint). You need it in Step 7.

 

Under Manage Configuration, Connections, choose Allow all IP addresses for the lab.

 

For anything beyond a lab, allow only your trusted IP range.

Under User Management, create a database user for the agent messaging. In my lab it is DPA_MSG_USER .

 

I did not grant it any additional privileges.

Step 5 – Download the DP Agent

Download the SDI Data Provisioning Agent for Linux x86_64 from the SAP Development Tools page, Cloud Integration tab.

 

Step 6 – Install the DP Agent on SLES

Unzip the installer and create a dedicated OS user and group:

 
bash
zypper install -y unzip
unzip installer.DPAgent-2.8.1.2-final-1-linuxx86_64.zip
groupadd -f dpagent
useradd -g dpagent -m -s /bin/bash dpagent
passwd dpagent

Create the target directory. Move the installer out of /root, because the dpagent user cannot read it there, and hand over the ownership:

 
bash
mkdir -p /usr/sap/dataprovagent
chown -R dpagent:dpagent /usr/sap/dataprovagent
mv /root/sapmedia/HANA_DP_AGENT_20_LIN_X86_64 /tmp/
chown -R dpagent:dpagent /tmp/HANA_DP_AGENT_20_LIN_X86_64
chmod -R 755 /tmp/HANA_DP_AGENT_20_LIN_X86_64

Switch to the agent user and start the installer:

 
bash
su - dpagent
cd /tmp/HANA_DP_AGENT_20_LIN_X86_64
./hdbinst

I accepted the defaults: installation path /usr/sap/dataprovagent, listener port 5050, administration port 5051 and the bundled JRE. The installer ends with Installation done.

 

The installer notes that the default settings use an insecure channel to the HANA server and that SSL must be configured afterwards. I kept the defaults for this lab.

Step 7 – Connect the configuration tool to SAP HANA Cloud

Start the configuration tool as the dpagent user:

 
bash
cd /usr/sap/dataprovagent/bin
./agentcli.sh --configAgent

Check that the agent runs with option 1, Agent Status, or start it with option 2, Start or Stop Agent. Then choose option 7, Connect the Configuration Tool to SAP HANA, and option 1, Connect to SAP HANA Cloud via JDBC .

 

Enter:

Prompt Value
Use encrypted JDBC connectiontrue
Host nameyour SQL endpoint, without the port
Port443
Use X509 client certificate (admin user)false
Agent admin HANA userDBADMIN
Use X509 client certificate (messaging user)false
HANA user for agent messagingDPA_MSG_USER
Use proxy serverfalse
Create a new SAP HANA userfalse, the user already exists

The tool answers Agent configuration tool is connected to SAP HANA server via JDBC.

Where this stops

Registering the agent option failed in my lab with:

 
text
SAP DBTech JDBC: [403]: internal error: Cannot connect to agent: dpagent_scc at <agent host>:5050
Context: Cannot connect to hdbdpserver

SAP KBA 3751584 describes this symptom and points to the dpserver service of the database not running. In SAP HANA Cloud Central, the Data Provisioning Server option under Advanced Settings is unchecked on my free tier instance, and I could not select it. SAP HANA Cloud Central also states that not all advanced options are available for free tier instances. I have not confirmed that the free tier is the cause, so I am not drawing that conclusion here.

I will continue with the registration and the adapters in a later post. If you have enabled the Data Provisioning Server on a free tier instance, I would be glad to hear how in the comments.

Conclusion

In this guide I prepared an SAP HANA Cloud free tier instance, installed the SAP HANA Data Provisioning Agent 2.8.1.2 on SLES 15 SP6, and connected the agent configuration tool to the database via JDBC.

A few points are worth remembering if you try the same:

  • SAP HANA Cloud Central needs its own tools subscription and the SAP HANA Cloud role collections. Missing either one shows up as No subscription or Not authorized.
  • Run the installer as a dedicated dpagent user, and keep the installer files somewhere that user can read.
  • When you copy commands from a terminal, leave the prompt out. A pasted > can overwrite a script.
  • The configuration tool connecting successfully does not mean the agent can be registered. Registration also needs the Data Provisioning Server of the database, and on my free tier instance I could not enable it.

entry.title: A Battery Recall, a Graph, and an AI Agent
entry.content:
This is a personal portfolio project exploring graph capabilities of the SAP HANA database. It tries to answer two questions: can a graph find everyone affected by a motorcycle battery recall, and can an AI Agent make a sensible remedy plan when replacement battery packs are scarce.

 

I asked Claude Code (Opus 5.5) what would be a good showcase for a graph. He suggested we do a spike first: a quick, throwaway experiment to see whether an idea holds water before anyone builds anything.

 

Spike one: The where-used index

The first candidate was ABAP's own where-used index. Table WBCROSSGT has 9.7 million rows on my A4H, and as a graph of who uses which type it came to 205,145 vertices and 1,017,224 edges. Unknown depth, cycles, the lot. Surely a job for a graph?

Turns out, not really. A plain ABAP loop of about 25 lines (level by level, SELECT ... FOR ALL ENTRIES, a hashed table of what it had already seen) found exactly the same objects in all four test cases, within about 2 seconds and with no setup. Warm, the graph was 3 to 8 times faster, but building it cold took 7 to 14 seconds. And the one job that should have been its home turf, finding cycles, gave no answer after 9 minutes, so we aborted it.

So much for that.

 

Spike two: The real-life project

Then I remembered a project I once did.

  • A manufacturing component is found to be defective.
  • Find all production orders where it was used,
  • then find the subsequent production orders where the material produced in the previous one was used as a component (several levels deep),
  • then find the sales orders where it was sold,
  • then find out whether it was shipped to a customer or is still at a storage location.

The objective: notify the customer and send them a replacement, or take the product out of the storage location and scrap it.

Would that have been a good case for a graph? We had no data to try it on. So we invented some, and gave it a home in my Supply Chain Rescue demo app, which already has a fictional maker of electric motorcycles. Electric motorcycles have batteries. Batteries have cell lots. You can see where this is going.

A second spike on that idea went better, so we built the real thing: Recall Rescue.

 

The battery genealogy

Claude generated 12 weeks of motorcycle production and sales, from week 28 of 2026, with a battery genealogy behind every one of them:

  • a cell lot from the supplier VoltCell goes into battery modules,
  • modules go into packs,
  • packs go into motorcycles, or wait at the service stock as spare packs,
  • motorcycles go to customers, or wait at a plant, a dealer or the service stock.

That alone would be a tree: every module sits in one pack and every pack in one motorcycle, so from any module there is exactly one way forward. What breaks the simple tree is reuse and remanufacturing:

  • On 1 September, 8 private motorcycles from week 29 got a new pack.
  • Their old packs were taken apart, and 2 modules each from 2 old packs made one remanufactured pack.

So now a module has two links:

  1. the old one to the pack it came from,
  2. the new one to the remanufactured pack.

On 21 September, 3 of the remanufactured packs went into motorcycles sold in weeks 31 to 35, under warranty. The old links stay in the database as history, marked inactive, and that will matter in a minute.

A perfect setup to declare one lot defective and try to trace it.

Side note: the EU thinks along the same lines. From 18 February 2027 every LMT and electric vehicle battery placed on the EU market, electric motorcycle batteries included, needs a battery passport, and a remanufactured battery gets "a new battery passport linked to the battery passport or passports of the original battery or batteries" (Article 77 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542). Recall Rescue doesn't build passports, mind you, but the links behind them make a graph for the same reason the workshop does here.

 

All in all 27,814 items and 42,487 links in two Database Tables in A4H, generated from a fixed seed, so the world comes out the same every time.

 

Four lines of openCypher

If you haven't met openCypher yet: it's a query language for graphs, the open version of Cypher, which came from Neo4j. Where SQL makes you join tables, openCypher has you draw the pattern you're looking for, in ASCII art. (a) is a node, -[r]-> is a relationship pointing from one node to the next, and [*1..4] means 1 to 4 relationships, whatever lies in between (the part that takes a loop in ABAP).

  • MATCH draws the pattern,
  • WHERE filters it,
  • RETURN says what you want back.

HANA understands a subset of it and runs it against a graph workspace.

The question for a recall is: who has a battery with cells from this lot, right now? In openCypher it reads almost like the sentence (RETURN trimmed):

MATCH p = (l)-[*1..4]->(u), (u)-[h]->(t)
WHERE l.VERTEXID = 'LOT-VC-W29-03' AND (u.KIND = 'VIN' OR u.KIND = 'PACK') AND (t.KIND = 'CUST' OR t.KIND = 'SLOC')
  AND h.ACTIVE = 'X' AND ALL(e IN RELATIONSHIPS(p) WHERE e.ACTIVE = 'X')
RETURN u.VERTEXID AS UNIT, t.VERTEXID AS HOLDER

Start at the lot, follow 1 to 4 links to a motorcycle or a pack, then one more link to whoever holds it - a customer or a storage location. Current links only.

That last condition is important. For the lot LOT-VC-W29-03 the trace finds 27 units with their holders. Let it follow the history too, and it finds 35: Eight customers would get a recall notice for a battery that isn't in their motorcycle any more.

This is what the trace has to walk through: the whole family tree of LOT-VC-W29-03, straight from the vertex and edge tables, history and all. The red dashed links are the 8 packs the workshop took out, and the grey motorcycles are the 8 customers who would get a notice for nothing:

And this is what the four lines of openCypher make of it, as the app draws their answer: 27 units with their holders, 4 of them through the remanufactured packs, and not one of the 8 grey motorcycles:

How do I know the graph isn't just confidently wrong? Claude also wrote an oracle: a plain JavaScript walk over the same items and links, level by level, with no graph anywhere. For all 8 standard lots of week 29 the two agree exactly, unit by unit and holder by holder.

And speed? Doesn't matter at this size. In the spike the ABAP loop took 77 ms and the graph 67 ms. Now a warm trace answers in about 400 to 800 ms, through OData and all. Here is a screenshot from Postman:

 

The catch

There is one, and it's big if you live in ABAP Cloud.

  • The trace runs on A4H's own HANA, over a graph workspace that an AMDP method defines on two CDS view entities.
  • But openCypher won't go through an AMDP. ABAP's check rejects the SQL that HANA expands the query into: "The ABAP database schema ... cannot be specified explicitly". Uwe Fetzer ( @UweFetzer_se38 ) reported exactly this back in 2019, in his SAP Community question Opencypher in AMDP, and SAP called it a bug. I hit the same error on my release 816 system.
  • What does work is native SQL through ADBC (cl_sql_statement): SELECT ... FROM OPENCYPHER_TABLE( GRAPH WORKSPACE ... QUERY '...' ). ADBC is not released for ABAP Cloud, so this is classic ABAP only.
  • No query parameters either. The lot goes into the query text, so it's checked against a strict pattern first, and nothing but a lot number of the form LOT-VC-W29-03 gets through.
  • HANA 2.00.087 speaks a subset of openCypher: no named variable-length edge like [e*1..4], and one hop per pattern element. Hence the comma in the MATCH above.

The trace is a RAP custom entity, so to everyone else it's just another OData entity set.

 

Inside ZCL_RR_TRACE

The whole graph part lives in one class, ZCL_RR_TRACE. The graph itself is ten lines of it, an AMDP method that says which CDS view entity holds the vertices and which the edges:

METHOD graph BY DATABASE GRAPH WORKSPACE FOR HDB
  LANGUAGE SQL
  USING zi_rr_graphedge zi_rr_graphvertex.
  edge table zi_rr_graphedge
    source column sourceid
    target column targetid
    key    column edgeid
  vertex table zi_rr_graphvertex
    key    column vertexid
ENDMETHOD.

ZI_RR_GraphVertex reads the items, ZI_RR_GraphEdge the links. No copy of the data, no extra tables. Apart from that, the class does three jobs:

  1. It wakes the graph up. HANA creates an AMDP graph workspace only the first time an AMDP uses it, and our query comes in through ADBC. So before every query a tiny GraphScript procedure (HANA's own graph language) counts the vertices. The count goes nowhere - it's the wake-up call.
  2. It asks the question. Method UNITS checks the lot against the pattern, writes the four lines of openCypher into a string, wraps them in SELECT ... FROM OPENCYPHER_TABLE( GRAPH WORKSPACE "ZCL_RR_TRACE=>GRAPH" QUERY '...' ) and runs that through cl_sql_statement. The graph answers with units and holders only. Plain ABAP SQL then adds the model, the pack type, the delivery date, the current pack and the modules for the route text.
  3. It serves OData. The class implements IF_RAP_QUERY_PROVIDER, which makes it the query behind the custom entity ZI_RR_Trace. It takes exactly two filters, LotId eq and WithHistory eq, refuses any sorting, and does the paging itself.

 

The rest of the plumbing

Around the trace:

  • a RAP business object for the recall, in A4H: declare a lot defective, own the affected units (so two recalls never fight over one motorcycle), apply a remedy plan all or nothing,
  • in CAP, the plan and its rules: spare packs are scarce, so customers come first, and no motorcycle in stock gets a pack while a customer waits for one,
  • a Recall Agent who proposes a plan, explains it, and waits for an approver before anything reaches A4H,
  • a Recall section in the app, with the trace drawn as a graph and a button that opens the existing battery shortage scenario. One defect, two directions: back to who is affected, forward to what the shortage stops.

This is the trace of LOT-VC-W29-03 in the app, with the fleet customer CUS-FLEET-2 clicked: its routes light up in blue and everything else fades. 3 motorcycles, one of them through the remanufactured pack PCK-R0002, whose line stays orange. The modules are tucked into the lines from the lot to the packs:

In the first end-to-end run, the Recall Agent (Claude Sonnet 5) got LOT-VC-W29-03: 23 customer motorcycles, 3 in stock, 1 spare pack, 4 routes through remanufactured packs, and 16 free spare packs to go round. About 50 seconds later he was waiting for approval, with a plan:

  • 16 customers get a replacement pack now,
  • 7 get a notice and wait,
  • the 3 motorcycles in stock are blocked,
  • the affected spare pack is scrapped,
  • 10 packs need new supply from VoltCell, which in the Supply Chain Rescue world is blocked.

He also explained why one of the 6 fleet motorcycles, delivered two weeks after the other 5, doesn't jump the queue: "bumping it ahead of earlier-committed customers isn't justified by any stated operational need".

On the trace, a plan shows in colour: green gets a new pack now, purple waits for new supply, with the delivery date that decides who comes first. This is the bottom of the motorcycles column for that plan, the same as the rule plan. VIN-CARGO-31034, delivered on 6 August, waits in purple, while the other fleet motorcycles from 23 July get their packs:

Did the Agent do anything the rule plan didn't? Not this time: 0 units differ. After Approve, the plan was applied in A4H in 5.5 seconds.

Then Claude ran it again for the screenshots: same lot, same world, same Model. And this time that fleet motorcycle did jump the queue:

 

2 units differ from the rule plan: the fleet motorcycle VIN-CARGO-31034 got PCK-003635, the pack the rule plan gives to VIN-CITY-29118, and VIN-CITY-29118 waits instead. The Agent's reason: fleet vehicles "see higher daily mileage/usage and are safety-prioritized for scarce replacement packs ahead of equally-dated non-fleet customers".

Equally dated? VIN-CITY-29118 was delivered on 23 July, VIN-CARGO-31034 on 6 August. And Approve? Claude clicked it, taking the screenshots for me in the browser, without checking the dates either.

So which rule did the Agent break? None, strictly speaking. The delivery date is only the order the rule plan goes by. What the app enforces is that customers come before motorcycles in stock and that no spare pack sits idle while someone waits, and A4H checks the rest when the plan is applied. Fleet first is even allowed: the Agent's instructions say he may change which customers get the scarce packs, "for example fleet motorcycles in daily use first", as long as he explains every difference from the rule plan. He did explain it. The explanation was just wrong.

What could be changed after seeing this? For example: show the delivery dates of the units that differ on the card, have CAP check the dates the rationale claims, or leave the app as it is and make sure a person reads the units that differ.

 

So, was the graph useful?

Not because of speed. At this size it decides nothing, and a plain loop keeps up. On the query, the recall question is four lines of openCypher, and the difference between the right notices and 8 wrong ones on top is one condition in those four lines. The catch is the platform: classic ABAP only, through native SQL, until the AMDP bug is fixed.

And the Agent? He made a plan that passed every rule, in about 50 seconds, and in one of two runs explained it with dates that weren't true. The rules caught nothing because nothing was broken. The reason would still probably need a person who checks it against the data, thought.

 

P.S.: The setup was A4H, the 2025 Developer Trial (release 816 on HANA 2.00.087), in Docker on a VPS, reached through an SSH tunnel, and a Mac. Claude Code ran Opus 5.5 as the main Agent, with Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5 sub-Agents, and talked to A4H through the vibing-steampunk MCP Server by Alice Vinogradova. Supply Chain Rescue runs CAP 10.1 on Node 24 and SAPUI5 1.136.8. The code: github.com/Kamilkov/supply-chain-rescue.

entry.title: Configuring SSL Encryption Between SAP ABAP Application Servers and SAP HANA
entry.content:
Introduction

This blog documents the steps required to configure SSL/TLS encryption between SAP ABAP application servers and an SAP HANA database, using a certificate signed by an external Certificate Authority (CA). This is a common requirement in enterprise migrations and security hardening projects where the default SAP-generated certificates are replaced with organisation-specific ones.

The configuration covered here implements TLS — the HANA database server authenticates itself to the ABAP application layer. sapcli.pse on each ABAP node serves as the trust store, allowing the ABAP kernel to verify HANA's certificate during the TLS handshake. This guide assumes you are working on a Linux-based SAP system with SAP CommonCryptoLib installed.

Prerequisites

  • Database certificate (.pfx format) signed by an external CA, plus the corresponding root certificate
  • Certificate password
  • Access to the HANA database server at OS level (sidadm or equivalent)
  • Access to all ABAP application server nodes at OS level
  • A valid HANA userstore key configured for hdbsql commands
  • Planned downtime or maintenance window — the ABAP application must be stopped during parts of this procedure
  • Existing SAPSSLS.pse backed up before making any changes

Overview

The procedure creates two sets of PSE (Personal Security Environment) files:

  1. SAPSSLS.pse on the HANA server — the HANA database server's SSL identity, built from the externally signed certificate. This is what HANA presents to the ABAP layer during the TLS handshake.

  2. sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse on each ABAP application server — these are placed in the sec directory of each ABAP node. They act as the trust store on the ABAP side, containing the CA certificate chain that the ABAP kernel uses to verify HANA's certificate. The sslKeyStore reference in the profile parameter also points to sapcli.pse, but since sslclientpki is off on HANA, the client certificate is never requested.

Step 1 — Upload Certificates to the HANA Server

  1. Log on to the HANA database server at OS level as sidadm
  2. Upload the database certificate (db_cert.pfx), the root certificate (root.cer) (and any intermediate certificates) to the sec directory on the HANA server:
/usr/sap/<SID>/SYS/global/security/rsecssls/

Note: The exact sec directory path may vary. Confirm the location using the SECUDIR environment variable.

  1. Before making any changes, back up the existing SAPSSLS.pse:
cp SAPSSLS.pse SAPSSLS.pse.bak

Step 2 — Create SAPSSLS.pse on the HANA Server

Run the following command to create a new SAPSSLS.pse from the externally signed certificate. This becomes the HANA server's SSL identity:

sapgenpse import_p12 -r root.cer -p SAPSSLS.pse <db_cert.pfx>
  • Enter the certificate password when prompted
  • When asked for a PIN, you have the option to set one or leave it empty. From a security perspective, setting a PIN is recommended as it adds an additional layer of protection to the PSE file. If a PIN is set, ensure it is stored securely as it will be required for any future PSE operations

SAPSSLS.pse should now be created successfully.

Step 3 — Create the Client PSE Files for ABAP Application Servers

sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse can be created directly from SAPSSLS.pse:

cp SAPSSLS.pse sapcli.pse
cp SAPSSLS.pse sapsrv.pse

Copy both files to the sec directory on every ABAP application server node (CS/CI and all additional application servers):

/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/

Step 4 — Disable sslclientpki on HANA

Important: Shut down the ABAP application layer before executing this step.

This parameter controls whether HANA enforces client PKI certificate authentication. Setting it to off enables one-way TLS (server authentication only), which is the configuration used here.

Run the following hdbsql command from the HANA server:

hdbsql -U <USERSTORE_KEY> "ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') SET ('communication', 'sslclientpki') = 'off' WITH RECONFIGURE;"

The WITH RECONFIGURE clause applies the change immediately without requiring a HANA restart.

PRD Systems: This parameter must also be disabled on the secondary/DR HANA node. This can be done via SAP HANA Studio — apply the change on both the primary and DR secondary database nodes.

Step 5 — Configure the ABAP Default Profile

The dbs/hdb/connect_property parameter must be added to the ABAP default profile (DEFAULT.PFL) to instruct the ABAP kernel to use SSL when connecting to HANA. This parameter applies to all application server instances.

Add the following parameter (adapt values to your system):

dbs/hdb/connect_property = ENCRYPT=TRUE,sslCryptoProvider=commoncrypto,sslKeyStore=/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/sapcli.pse,sslTrustStore=/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/sapcli.pse,sslHostNameInCertificate=<hana_hostname>.<yourdomain.com>

Key values to adapt:

  • <SID> — your system ID
  • <instance_dir> — the instance directory of each application server (e.g. D00, D01)
  • <hana_hostname>.<yourdomain.com> — the fully qualified hostname as it appears in the HANA certificate's CN/SAN field

Note: The sslHostNameInCertificate value must match exactly what is embedded in the HANA server certificate, otherwise the SSL handshake will fail.

Step 6 — Restart the Application and Validate

Start the ABAP application layer. Once all instances are up, perform the following validation steps.

Validation 1 — Check encrypted connections via SQL

Log on to the system and navigate to transaction DB02 → SQL Editor. Run the following statement, replacing <SCHEMA> with the correct database schema name:

SELECT IS_ENCRYPTED, SSL_VERSION, CLIENT_HOST
FROM SYS.M_CONNECTIONS
WHERE USER_NAME = '<SCHEMA>'
AND IS_ENCRYPTED = 'TRUE';

All active connections for the schema should return TRUE in the IS_ENCRYPTED column. If any sessions return FALSE, review the profile parameter and PSE file placement.

Validation 2 — R3trans connectivity check

Run the following from the OS level on each application server to confirm no transport-layer issues:

R3trans -d

Review the trans.log output — a clean run with no errors confirms successful connectivity between the ABAP application layer and HANA over SSL.

Summary

At this point, SSL encryption between the SAP ABAP application servers and SAP HANA is active using an externally signed CA certificate. The HANA server authenticates to the application layer via SAPSSLS.pse, while each ABAP node uses sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse as its trust store for verifying HANA's identity.

This guide was produced by the IT Planning and Software Logistics team, SAP Ireland, based on field experience from enterprise RISE migration projects.

entry.title: ACDOCA Partitioning: Plan for Growth Before the Next Downtime Window
entry.content:
Introduction

A growing partition can need attention just when the business can't spare a long outage. The best opportunity to avoid that squeeze is before go-live, when there is still room to test a layout against future growth. Using ACDOCA as the example, I look at that early design decision and the harder choice on an existing system: whether native repartitioning or a staged rebuild with SAP Landscape Transformation Replication Server (SLT) can fit the available capacity and business window.

Large tables can become a major operational pain point. In S/4HANA, ACDOCA deserves particular attention because financial posting and reporting depend on it. Review its growth, partition balance and maintenance requirements regularly, before capacity or downtime constraints narrow the options. The same discipline applies to other large SAP HANA tables.

1. Design for growth before go-live

On a new implementation, bring the finance team and HANA administrators into the partition discussion before the bulk load. Estimate journal-line growth, migration volumes, retention and peak posting activity, then test the proposed layout against the reports and business transactions that matter. Give someone responsibility for reviewing growth after go-live. SAP's design guidance calls for testing both select and insert performance as data changes. [1]

Hash partitioning aims to distribute rows across partitions. Range partitioning groups values into intervals, such as periods; its effectiveness depends on the actual distribution. A multilevel layout can combine distribution and range requirements. More partitions also create administrative and query overhead, so a high partition count needs a clear purpose. [2]

For a large ACDOCA with period-driven reporting, I'd start by testing a range-based layout and checking whether the main queries actually prune partitions. Then I'd size the largest planned range before choosing its boundaries and the partition count.

Projected rows per range ≈ projected ACDOCA rows per period × periods in the range. Where volumes vary, sum the period-specific projections instead. Include existing rows and expected additions through the planning horizon, including late postings into older periods. Count physical ACDOCA rows across the relevant ledgers, rather than assuming one business journal line equals one row.

Compare the largest projected range with the operational threshold described below. If it approaches that threshold, test narrower ranges first. When even one period is too large, or finer ranges create excessive overhead, my next candidate is a multilevel layout that also uses hash distribution within each range. Column and key restrictions can require multilevel partitioning before capacity does. Check the current finance guidance in SAP Note 2289491 and partitioning FAQ 2044468 before choosing FISCYEARPER, BELNR, the level order or a single-level definition. [3] [4]

SAP documents a maximum of 2,147,483,648 rows per column-store partition for HANA 2.0 SPS 08. Set an operational threshold well below that boundary, based on growth and the time needed to complete another change. [5] SAP's administration training suggests up to 1.5 billion rows when addressing the row limit, with fewer where substantial growth is expected. That isn't a fixed target for every ACDOCA system. [2]

A range design needs an owner for future ranges and the OTHERS partition. Adding a range can move matching data out of OTHERS, which becomes expensive if it has accumulated many rows. [2] For other large tables, check application ownership of partition management as well: SAP BW, for example, manages its own partitioning. [1]

2. Reassess the existing partition layout

For an established system, first identify what's forcing the change. A fast-growing partition, uneven distribution, reporting latency and a difficult maintenance window lead to different tests. Compare the current and candidate layouts using representative data and workload, then choose how to carry out the change.

Route When it fits

Native offline repartitioningThe operation and its recovery allowance fit the measured capacity and business window.
Native online partitioningThe revision supports the required change, and rehearsal shows acceptable locking, temporary resource use and business response.
SLT with a prepared replacementMoving the copy ahead of cutover addresses the window constraint, and the application-specific switch is supported and rehearsed.

Start by testing the native route. If its resource demands, elapsed time and recovery allowance fit, there's a strong case for keeping the change within HANA's partitioning operation. If the copy work can't fit the window, evaluate an SLT rebuild with SAP and establish whether staging, change catch-up and reconciliation can run alongside business activity. Table size alone doesn't settle that choice.

Start with this read-only snapshot in the relevant tenant database. Replace YOUR_SCHEMA with the application schema and adapt the table filter for another column-store table. The queries require monitoring privileges and use HANA 2.0 SPS 08 view definitions. Memory values use GiB, calculated as bytes divided by 1,073,741,824. [6]

SELECT HOST, PORT, PART_ID, IS_REPLICA, LOADED, RECORD_COUNT,
       ROUND(MEMORY_SIZE_IN_TOTAL / 1073741824.0, 2) AS TOTAL_GIB,
       ROUND(MEMORY_SIZE_IN_DELTA / 1073741824.0, 2) AS DELTA_GIB
FROM SYS.M_CS_TABLES
WHERE SCHEMA_NAME = 'YOUR_SCHEMA'
  AND TABLE_NAME = 'ACDOCA'
ORDER BY RECORD_COUNT DESC, HOST, PORT, PART_ID;

Read memory alongside LOADED, whose values are NO, PARTIALLY and FULL. A partition that is unloaded or only partly loaded can need more memory when additional columns are accessed; its current footprint doesn't tell you how many rows it holds. Keep host, port and replica status with each observation. Delta memory is already included in total memory, so don't add it again. [6] SAP also warns that some memory estimates can show zero after a split or merge until a delta merge updates them. Interpret those values with the operation's state. [7]

3. Size and rehearse the native SQL operation

Before estimating a change, establish what “table size” measures: persisted data, loaded table memory or another metric. Then measure what the proposed operation adds while the rest of the database is running. SAP documents memory-allocation failures during repartitioning and treats additional disk space as a separate question. [8] [9]

One check is easy to miss: the memory available to the host and the memory allowed to a statement are separate constraints. HANA can stop a statement when its applicable memory limit is reached. User settings and workload-class mappings need review alongside the HANA allocation limits, including the threshold that controls when a statement limit applies. [10] [11] Record the effective settings used in rehearsal and check the production execution context against them.

The rehearsal should cover the proposed layout at representative scale, including data skew and the competing workload. Record elapsed time, peak host and statement memory, CPU, data and log growth, and business response. Include abort and recovery time in the maintenance plan. A run that finishes just before the window closes leaves little room for an unexpected result.

Use SAP KBA 3215774 as a reference for monitoring and investigating a long-running repartitioning operation. [12] Native online partitioning can reduce lock duration, but the exact operation and revision still matter. SAP also documents an online-partitioning failure associated with a statement-memory limit during replica synchronization. [13] [14]

4. Move the copy ahead of cutover where SLT fits

An SLT-based design can prepare a partitioned replacement while the original continues serving the business. That leaves the final outage to cover remaining changes, reconciliation, the application-table switch and validation. The benefit has a capacity cost: both paths have to run together during the copy.

For an application-owned table such as ACDOCA, establish the supported switch and recovery procedure with SAP for the relevant release. Include ABAP Dictionary consistency, indexes, dependencies and downstream consumers. Replication documentation on its own doesn't establish that an application table can be replaced with a replica.

Check target creation and refresh behavior before loading. In Advanced Replication Settings (transaction LTRS), a partition command can be supplied for table creation, while refresh options can recreate a prepared target. SAP also describes S/4HANA scenarios in which Alternative Table Name is unavailable. Validate the actual mapping and target behavior in the proposed configuration. [15]

Figure 1. Conceptual reading-type-5 example showing the original, replacement and applicable staging store. A supported application-table switch and recovery procedure are prerequisites.

5. Plan for memory, disk and processing capacity

During a staged rebuild, the live table, growing replacement and any resident staging data may share the same HANA host. Extraction and inserts also need working memory. Merges add another overlap: SAP describes the original main storage remaining available while a new main is built and new changes enter a second delta. Size the affected partitions and concurrent merges, rather than assuming a fixed multiplier for the whole database. [16]

Build separate disk and memory budgets

Collect synchronized measurements through loading, catch-up and recovery. Start from the normal host baseline, identify the additional allocations, and compare the combined observations with service and host totals. Count the live table once. Keep persisted staging bytes separate from staging memory, and use consistent decimal TB or binary TiB units.

Resource Evidence to collect

Table persistenceSource, replacement and staging disk bytes, their locations and how long they coexist.
Resident table memoryLoaded source, replacement and staging memory; main and delta counted once.
Additional working memoryChange queues, extraction and load buffers, and merge or compression allocations outside the table totals.
Storage capacityUsed and allocated data volumes, log growth, free filesystem space and recovery requirements.
Processing and business responseCPU, I/O latency, sustained throughput, replication lag and transaction response times.

Here is a separate persistence query. Its disk bytes describe table data at each listed location; filesystem consumption also includes allocated volume space, logs and other files. [17]

SELECT HOST, PORT, PART_ID,
       ROUND(DISK_SIZE / 1073741824.0, 2) AS DISK_GIB
FROM SYS.M_TABLE_PERSISTENCE_LOCATION_STATISTICS
WHERE SCHEMA_NAME = 'YOUR_SCHEMA'
  AND TABLE_NAME = 'ACDOCA'
ORDER BY DISK_SIZE DESC, HOST, PORT, PART_ID;

At the busiest point, compare source, replacement, staging and working allocations that actually coexist. Adding each component's highest value from a different time can overstate simultaneous consumption. Reserve further capacity for workload variation and recovery, then check the effective HANA limits and physical host capacity, allowing separately for the operating system. Remote source, target and SLT hosts need their own budgets.

Measure throughput alongside resource use

More parallel jobs help only while useful throughput improves and business response remains acceptable. Reading, serialization, inserts, compression and merges consume resources at different points in the run. SAP's merge-token mechanism ties merge scheduling to available resources. [18]

For a hypothetical initial load of 12 billion rows, a sustained rate of 100,000 rows per second gives 33.3 hours: 12 billion ÷ 100,000 ÷ 3,600. At 50,000 rows per second, the same arithmetic gives 66.7 hours. These illustrative rates exclude setup, change catch-up, reconciliation and cutover; use measured throughput for the actual plan.

A 24-hour query filter won't cover a load that runs for several days. For a multi-day rehearsal, use _SYS_STATISTICS.HOST_DELTA_MERGE_STATISTICS; the example below looks back seven days. SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 08 documents 42 days of history with a 300-second collection interval. Check collection and retention before the run so the history covers the whole exercise. [19]

SELECT SNAPSHOT_ID, HOST, PORT, PART_ID, START_TIME,
       TYPE, MOTIVATION,
       ROUND(EXECUTION_TIME / 1000.0, 2) AS DURATION_SECONDS,
       SUCCESS, LAST_ERROR, ERROR_DESCRIPTION
FROM _SYS_STATISTICS.HOST_DELTA_MERGE_STATISTICS
WHERE SCHEMA_NAME = 'YOUR_SCHEMA'
  AND TABLE_NAME = 'ACDOCA'
  AND TYPE IN ('MERGE', 'SPARSE')
  AND START_TIME >= ADD_DAYS(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, -7)
ORDER BY START_TIME DESC, HOST, PORT, PART_ID, SNAPSHOT_ID;

The filter includes delta merges and compression optimization, excluding hint records whose status has a different meaning. An unsuccessful call needs its error description: a call can decide that no merge is necessary. For recent activity, SYS.M_DELTA_MERGE_STATISTICS remains useful before the next history collection. [20] START_TIME is the operation's start time; SNAPSHOT_ID is the UTC collection timestamp. Align timestamps with host and service telemetry when investigating peaks, and don't count repeated observations of one operation as separate merges. [19]

6. Watch staging growth during the initial load

Track sender staging and the replacement table separately during the initial load. A queue can keep growing while the target is still loading, adding pressure to the host even when extraction looks healthy. Compare queue growth, target throughput, replication lag and business response on the same timeline before increasing concurrency.

The SAP SLT Performance Optimization Guide, document version 2.2 dated 2025-10-08, identifies DMC_INDXCL for legacy sender-queue reading types 4/5 and DHCDC_RTSTORE for subscription-based reading type 5. It describes staging growth during initial load and deletion after completion. The guide's pooled- and cluster-table space estimates are not an ACDOCA sizing rule. [21]

The staging-store name changed between guide versions. The 2021 guide names DMC_INDXCL in its subscription-based section; the 2025 guide uses DHCDC_RTSTORE there. Match observations to the component versions and recording mechanism. [22] [21]

Figure 2. Conceptual reading-type-5 lifecycle with separate qualitative scales. The curves show no production measurements or sizing ratio, and queue cleanup does not predict when allocated data-volume files shrink.

The 2025 guide also describes subscription-based reading type 1, which avoids intermediate payload staging in DHCDC_RTSTORE, subject to prerequisites and a transfer-time trade-off. Test the eligible reading methods for your components. [21] After an interruption, follow the cleanup or restart procedure for that method: SAP documents initial-load errors after DMC_INDXCL entries are removed. [23]

Deleting staging records and reclaiming physical disk space are separate events. Check both used and allocated data-volume space and the revision's reclaim behavior. Include that distinction in the recovery plan so cleanup isn't mistaken for immediately available filesystem capacity. [24]

7. Reconcile before reopening the business

Begin reconciliation during rehearsal and leave time to investigate differences, correct them and repeat the comparison. A matching total count can still conceal missing, extra or differing records. Define key-level comparisons and business totals, including the treatment of deletes, archiving and any filters. SAP's Cross-Database Comparison integration provides a useful reference for data-level comparison. [25]

Monitor outstanding changes, their age and replication latency as the cutover approaches. [26] A finished initial load is one milestone; the decision to proceed also depends on consistent data, a manageable backlog and time to complete the application checks.

During the cutover window, stop business writers and drain active transactions while keeping the runtime required to apply final changes available. Complete the consistency checks and rehearsed switch sequence, validate application access and downstream behavior, then reopen. Set a go/no-go deadline that preserves time for recovery and confirm the required backup and recovery prerequisites before starting.

A retained original table needs particular care. Once postings resume against the replacement, the retained copy becomes stale. Recovery must account for those new transactions; renaming the old table back can't, by itself, restore a consistent current state.

Conclusion

Start the next partition change while there's still time to test it. Whether the table is ACDOCA or another large business table, choose a route that rehearsal shows can complete the cutover, or recover if needed, within the business window. Which constraint is boxing you in right now: partition growth, memory headroom, replication catch-up or the window?

Tell me in the comments, or send me a message about the trade-off you're working through.

SAP references

References checked October 2026. The technical scope is SAP HANA Platform 2.0, including SPS 08, and SLT. Confirm operations, view definitions and settings against your HANA revision, S/4HANA release and SLT components. Full SAP Notes and KBA resolutions may require SAP for Me access; their current full text must be checked before implementation. These read-only SQL examples support observation, not a prescribed ACDOCA partition definition.

entry.title: CDS View Performance Best Practice – UNION in a LEFT OUTER JOIN
entry.content:
UNION in a LEFT OUTER JOIN -  CDS (SQL) performance anti-pattern

This blog post focuses on the CDS view performance anti-pattern called "UNION in LEFT OUTER JOIN" and it's part of the CDS View Performance Best Practices series. You can find an introduction to CDS View performance recommendations, aspects you need to consider in terms of performance, and a list of all available CDS anti-patterns in the following blog post: 
CDS View Performance Best Practices 

 

Why this pattern deserves attention

A UNION in the right-hand input of a LEFT OUTER JOIN is logically valid. The risk is performance: on large data volumes and complex data models, both UNION branches may be processed before a selective filter from the left side of the join can reduce them. In simple and highly selective cases, the optimizer may apply semi-join reduction. In more complex plans, that optimization is not guaranteed because plan selection is cost based.

 

The business example

A retail company tracks customer orders for multiple sales regions. Each order is fulfilled through one of two independent delivery systems: a central warehouse or a regional warehouse. Fulfillment is exclusive in this model: an order is only assigned to one delivery system. Some orders are still open and therefore have no delivery record. The data below is intentionally minimal so that result of every row can be easily followed through each query variant by hand.

Data model

The following three tables are created and populated by the complete runnable SQL at the end of this post. All rows are shown so every query result can be verified by hand.

The original, correct query

The query goal is to list every order together with its delivery date from Region 2 (region_id = 2), regardless of which delivery system handled it. Open orders must still appear with a NULL delivery date — the LEFT OUTER JOIN is the mechanism that guarantees this.

with deliveries as (
    select order_id, delivery_date
      from central_deliveries
    union all
    select order_id, delivery_date
      from regional_deliveries
)
select o.order_id,
       o.region_id,
       d.delivery_date
  from orders o
  left outer join deliveries d
    on o.order_id = d.order_id
 where o.region_id = 2;

Please note that the query uses a common table expression (CTE). The with_clause creates a temporary result set based on its subquery. The native SQL approach uses the WITH clause for simplicity, avoiding multiple view definitions and lengthy code snippets while showing the essence of the anti-pattern in a single executable statement.

Technically, this has the same effect as when a CDS view uses an association (technically a LEFT OUTER JOIN) to another CDS view that contains a UNION.

 The main query selects from the table ORDERS and uses the temporary view (CTE) DELIVERIES in a LEFT OUTER JOIN. The CTE  DELIVERIES contains a UNION ALL of the two delivery tables CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES.

Correct and expected result of the query:

REGION_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

Let’s look at the execution plan for the query.

The plan places the UNION ALL below the LEFT OUTER JOIN, this means the UNION ALL is executed before the LEFT OUTER JOIN. The filtered ORDERS table is the left input, while CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES are combined as the right input.

The UNION ALL combines the rows from both delivery tables so that an order can match a delivery stored in either table. The LEFT OUTER JOIN then keeps every selected Region 2 order, including ORD400, for which neither table contains a delivery record.

The plan does not show the selected order IDs being used to reduce the scans of CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES. Rows that cannot match a selected order are therefore processed.

Can the filtered ORDERS input and the LEFT OUTER JOIN be pushed into the individual UNION ALL branches to reduce the data earlier?

 

The tempting but incorrect rewrite

At first glance, it may seem attractive to push the filtered ORDERS input and the LEFT OUTER JOIN into each UNION ALL branch:

with deliveries_wrong_opt as (
    select o.order_id, o.region_id,
           cd.delivery_date
      from orders o
      left outer join central_deliveries cd
        on o.order_id = cd.order_id
     where o.region_id = 2
    union all
    select o.order_id, o.region_id,
           rd.delivery_date
      from orders o
      left outer join regional_deliveries rd
        on o.order_id = rd.order_id
     where o.region_id = 2
)
select * from deliveries_wrong_opt;

Why it fails: Each LEFT OUTER JOIN independently preserves every selected order. ORD300 has a matching row in CENTRAL_DELIVERIES, but not in REGIONAL_DELIVERIES therefore the regional branch produces a NULL-extended row for it. ORD500 has the symmetric problem. ORD400 has no match in either delivery table, so both branches produce a NULL-extended row for it.

The UNION ALL then combines the independently produced branch results. Consequently, the rewritten query returns six rows instead of the expected three. The additional rows are not caused by UNION ALL itself; they arise because each LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched orders independently.

REGION_ID

The execution plan shows both the performance appeal and the structural problem of this rewrite:

The UNION ALL is now above two separate LEFT OUTER JOIN operators. Each branch reads the filtered Region 2 rows from ORDERS and joins them independently with one delivery table: the first branch with CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and the second with REGIONAL_DELIVERIES. Because only the selected orders participate in each join, fewer rows may be passed from the join branches into the UNION ALL.

The earlier reduction therefore looks attractive from a performance perspective, but it changes the result. Because both joins are LEFT OUTER JOINs, each branch preserves all three Region 2 orders before the branch results are combined. A match in one branch does not prevent the other branch from producing a NULL-extended row for the same order. For this data set, the UNION ALL consequently receives three rows from each branch and returns the six rows shown above.

If the LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot be pushed down into the UNION ALL branches, can the delivery tables still be reduced earlier without changing the result?

 

A semantics-preserving manual reduction

The LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot safely be pushed down into the UNION ALL branches. Therefore, we describe an approach where the selected order IDs can be used to reduce each delivery table before the tables are combined.

The query first creates selected_order_keys, containing the order IDs for Region 2. Each delivery table is then joined with these IDs, so only deliveries for the selected orders enter the UNION ALL. The LEFT OUTER JOIN remains in the main query and therefore still returns open orders, such as ORD400, exactly once.

with selected_order_keys as (
    select distinct order_id
      from orders
     where region_id = 2
),
reduced_deliveries as (
    select d.order_id, d.delivery_date
      from central_deliveries d
      inner join selected_order_keys k
        on k.order_id = d.order_id
    union all
    select d.order_id, d.delivery_date
      from regional_deliveries d
      inner join selected_order_keys k
        on k.order_id = d.order_id
)
select o.order_id,
       o.region_id,
       d.delivery_date
  from orders o
  left outer join reduced_deliveries d
    on d.order_id = o.order_id
 where o.region_id = 2;

The DISTINCT ensures that each order ID occurs only once in selected_order_keys. Otherwise, duplicate IDs could multiply matching rows in the delivery tables.

This query produces the correct and expected result:

ORDER_ID

REGION_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

ORD300

2

2026-09-15

ORD400

2

NULL

ORD500

2

2026-09-18

The result remains the same as for the original query, but unrelated delivery rows are removed before the UNION ALL. The execution plan below shows how SAP HANA implements this reduction.

The filtered Region 2 order IDs are produced once by the DISTINCT operator and reused as a shared subplan. Each delivery table is then reduced through a HASH JOIN (SEMI): only delivery rows whose ORDER_ID occurs in selected_order_keys are passed to the UNION ALL. The resulting delivery rows form the right-hand input of the final HASH JOIN (LEFT OUTER).

The semi-joins reduce the delivery branches without producing NULL-extended order rows. Preserving unmatched orders remains the responsibility of the single LEFT OUTER JOIN above the UNION ALL. The plan therefore combines early reduction with the same result semantics as the original query.

The manual rewrite makes the reduction explicit by deriving the relevant order IDs and using them to restrict both delivery branches.

But is this manual rewrite always necessary, or can SAP HANA derive the same semi-join reduction automatically?

 

How SAP HANA can apply semi-join reduction automatically

The fact that the LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot be pushed down does not automatically imply poor performance. SAP HANA can introduce semi-join reduction as an optimizer transformation without changing the SQL statement. Whether it does so is cost based and depends on estimated cardinalities, internal cost evaluation rules, selectivity, table sizes, statistics, and the complexity of the execution plan resulting from the surrounding data model.

In the small teaching example used so far, the delivery tables contain only a few rows. Reducing them first offers little or no cost advantage, so SAP HANA may reasonably retain the original plan.

With larger data volumes, reducing rows before the UNION ALL can provide enough benefit for the optimizer to choose semi-join reduction automatically. The following example demonstrates this with large SAP tables.

Example with large SAP tables

Table

Description

Approximate number of rows

TADIR

Directory of ABAP Repository objects. It provides the object type, object name, and package assignment.

7 million

DD03L

Contains field information for ABAP Dictionary tables and structures.

15 million

DD03ND

Contains field information for structured Dictionary objects, including objects related to CDS data definitions.

2.5 million

Purpose of the query

The query selects the names and types of table definitions (TABL) and CDS data definitions (DDLS) assigned to package FINS_CODING_BLOCK in TADIR. It combines field information from DD03L and DD03ND with UNION ALL and left-joins the result to the selected repository objects.

The LEFT OUTER JOIN ensures that repository objects without matching field information are still returned. Objects with multiple fields produce one result row per field.

with fields as (
    select d.tabname as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03l d

    union all

    select d.strucobjn as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03nd d
)
select t.object,
       t.obj_name,
       f.fieldname
  from tadir t
  left outer join fields f
    on f.objectname = t.obj_name
 where t.devclass = 'FINS_CODING_BLOCK'
   and t.object in ('TABL', 'DDLS');

Execution with automatic semi-join reduction

For runtime measurements we will use Plan Visualizer (PlanViz) instead of the explain plan. If we create the execution plan for the query using PlanViz we can find the following time measurements on the Overview tab in the execution summary section:

Execution Time (Elapsed): 4.524 ms
Execution Time (CPU): 3.771 ms

The Plan Graph view of the PlanViz looks like this:

The filtered TADIR input is evaluated once and reused as a shared subplan. The filter returns 48 rows, compared with an estimate (by the optimizer) of 12 rows (number in parentheses). The operator times shown in this Plan Graph are CPU times, not elapsed times.

SAP HANA uses this selective result to apply a TABLE SCAN SEMI JOIN to both branches below the UNION ALL. The semi-join on DD03L passes 222 rows to the UNION ALL, while the semi-join on DD03ND passes 196 rows. Only rows with an object name that occurs in the filtered TADIR result are passed to the UNION ALL.

The UNION ALL combines the two branch results into 418 rows. These rows form the right-hand input of the final HASH JOIN (LEFT OUTER), while the filtered TADIR result remains the left-hand input. The outer join therefore continues to preserve selected repository objects without matching field information.

The plan demonstrates automatic semi-join reduction: SAP HANA uses the selective left-side input to reduce both large field tables before their rows are combined, without moving the LEFT OUTER JOIN into the UNION ALL branches. The measured CPU time for this run is approximately 3.8 ms.

The plan shows that SAP HANA reduces both field tables before the UNION ALL. But how much work does this transformation avoid? To make the difference visible, we can execute the same statement once more with semi-join reduction disabled and compare the two PlanViz results.

Execution with automatic semi-join reduction disabled

To isolate the effect of semi-join reduction, the same statement was executed again with the hint NO_HEX_TABLE_SCAN_SEMI_JOIN that prevents the table-scan semi-join reduction in the individual UNION ALL branches. The hint is used only for demonstration; disabling the optimization is not recommended.

with fields as (
    select d.tabname as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03l d

    union all

    select d.strucobjn as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03nd d
)
select t.object,
       t.obj_name,
       f.fieldname
  from tadir t
  left outer join fields f
    on f.objectname = t.obj_name
 where t.devclass = 'FINS_CODING_BLOCK'
   and t.object in ('TABL', 'DDLS') 
WITH HINT( NO_HEX_TABLE_SCAN_SEMI_JOIN );

The following time measurements are from the overview in the execution summary:

Execution Time (Elapsed): 472.078 ms
Execution Time (CPU): 7,291.854 ms

Compared to the previous optimized execution we can see significantly higher times.


Execution Time (Elapsed): 4.524 ms
Execution Time (CPU): 3.771 ms

The Plan Graph view looks like this:

With branch-level semi-join reduction disabled, the filtered TADIR input is still evaluated once and reused as a shared subplan. The filter returns 48 rows.

The main difference is visible below the UNION ALL. Semi-join reduction has not disappeared completely, but it now occurs above the UNION ALL. Consequently, both large field tables are scanned and combined before the result is reduced to the selected object names. The DD03L scan returns 15,747,433 rows, while the DD03ND scan returns 2,495,229 rows.

These large branch results enter the UNION ALL before a HASH JOIN (SEMI) reduces the combined field data to the object names from the filtered TADIR input. The semi-join eventually reduces the data to 418 rows, but the reduction happens only after rows from both large tables have already been read and combined.

The resulting 418 rows form the right-hand input of the final HASH JOIN (LEFT OUTER). As in the optimized plan, the filtered TADIR result remains the left-hand input, so repository objects without matching field information are still preserved. The final result therefore remains unchanged. The measured CPU time for this run is approximately 7.3 s.

Comparison of the two executions

Measurement

Semi-join reduction enabled

Branch-level reduction disabled

Rows from DD03ND entering UNION ALL

Final result rows

Both executions return the same 418 rows, but the optimized plan reduces each field table before the UNION ALL. This avoids passing more than 18 million rows through the union and reduces CPU time from approximately 7.3 seconds to 3.8 milliseconds. But what can a developer do if SAP HANA does not apply semi-join reduction and the UNION branches become a performance bottleneck?

 

When semi-join reduction is not applied

Semi-join reduction is a cost-based optimizer decision. It may not be selected when the left-side filter is insufficiently selective, cardinality estimates are inaccurate, or join columns contain casts or calculations. The structure of the data model also matters: additional joins, aggregations, calculated fields, and nested (reusable) views can increase the complexity of the resulting execution plan and make the relationship between the selective input and the UNION branches harder for the optimizer to identify.

This is one reason why controlling CDS model complexity is important. For broader guidance, see CDS View Performance Best Practices.

Use PlanViz with representative data volumes to check where rows are reduced, how many rows enter the UNION ALL, and whether estimated row counts differ significantly from the actual values.

What can a developer do?

  • If the branches use the same source rows at the same granularity and differ only in calculated values, consider replacing the union with a single source and CASE expressions. Verify that this preserves row multiplicity and NULL handling (see anti-pattern NOT NULL preserving LEFT OUTER JOIN).
  • Consider separate, more focused views when a broadly reusable union model prevents early filtering.
  • For expensive and stable combinations, consider whether a persisted or precomputed result is appropriate.
  • Verify every redesign with PlanViz and realistic production-scale data.

The objective is not to force a particular execution plan, but to shape the data model so that SAP HANA can reduce large data sets as early as possible.

 

Conclusion

A UNION ALL on the right side of a LEFT OUTER JOIN is logically valid, but it can become expensive when large union branches are processed before the selective left-side input reduces them. Simply moving the LEFT OUTER JOIN into the individual branches is not a safe optimization and leads to a semantically different result, because each branch would preserve unmatched rows.

SAP HANA can avoid this work through semi-join reduction, restricting the union branches while keeping the LEFT OUTER JOIN above the UNION. If this optimization is not applied and the union becomes a performance bottleneck, review the CDS model for opportunities to reduce data earlier without changing row multiplicity or NULL handling. Use PlanViz with representative data volumes to identify the problem and verify any redesign.

entry.title: From Integration to Intelligence :Building enterprise-ready AI agents with Integration Suite & MCP
entry.content:
I have sat through a lot of agent demos this year. The pattern is usually the same. Someone types a request in plain English, the agent reads a purchase requisition, checks a budget, creates a purchase order in S/4HANA, emails the supplier, and posts a cheerful summary. The room claps. It is impressive.

Then I ask the question that integration people always ask: what happens on the 40,000th run? What happens when the supplier endpoint times out, when the mapping changes, when audit wants to know who approved what, or when the token bill arrives at the end of the month?

That is the gap between an agent that works in a demo and an agent that survives production. After close to two decades of building integrations, first on Oracle SOA and OSB, later on Boomi, Apigee and SAP BTP, my view is that the gap is mostly not a model problem. It is an architecture problem. And it is one the SAP integration community is unusually well placed to solve.

Last week I attended SAP's session "Building the Autonomous Enterprise with Integration Suite, AEM, and Agents" (13 October 2026). One line from it has stayed with me, because it captures the whole argument in eight words:

"Let the agent think. Let Integration Suite execute."

This post is my attempt to unpack that line from an architect's point of view: where agents earn their keep, where they should stay out of the way, and how API-centric integration and the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite connect the two.

1. The overloaded agent

When teams first build agents, they tend to give them everything. The agent calls the APIs, builds the payloads, decides on retries, transforms the formats and handles the errors. It feels efficient because there is only one component to think about.

It is not efficient. In effect you are asking a probabilistic reasoning engine to re-implement things your integration platform already does deterministically, with monitoring, retries and audit built in. Mapping JSON to IDoc, routing a message by company code, validating mandatory fields against a schema, sending a payment file over a bank channel: none of these need judgment. They need to be done exactly the same way every time.

The SAP session framed the consequences well, and they match what I have seen in practice:

  • Duplicated capability. The agent rebuilds APIs, EDI handling, mappings and routing you already own.
  • Reduced reliability. Predictable PO, invoice and payment flows start to depend on non-deterministic behavior.
  • Harder governance. Security, auditability and compliance become difficult to standardize when logic lives inside prompts.
  • Blurred accountability. When something fails, is it the reasoning, the integration, the partner or the backend? Nobody can tell quickly.
  • Higher operating cost. Tokens and agent capacity are spent on repetitive plumbing instead of the reasoning you actually wanted.

I like to describe it as driving a Lamborghini to the supermarket. You can, but it is not what the car is for, and the parking is a nightmare.

2. Who should own each step? A Procure-to-Pay test

The most useful part of the session, for me, was a simple step-by-step assessment of a standard Procure-to-Pay flow. For each step, it asked one question: is the value here in reasoning, or in reliable execution? I have adapted it below because I think every team should run this exercise on its own processes before writing a single prompt.

P2P step

Owner

Why

1

Create requisition

Medium

Agent

2

Approve requisition

Low

High

Agent

Summarize context and policy, recommend

3

Create purchase order

Very high

Integration Suite

Structured execution: APIs, EDI, mapping

4

Very high

Integration Suite

Receive, transform, update

5

6

Low

10
